name: Consistent sequencing under fatigue with maintained structure
target_behavior: deliberate action sequencing and tactical organization of offensive and defensive combinations
purpose: Head Movement develops evasive capabilities. Thursday maintains organized execution during complex, extended sequences under fatigue.
standard_setup: Pairs face each other at a distance where the feeder's punches stop short; run when athletes are already tired, at the point the session plan sets. The coach stands side-on.
execution:
Coach names a head-movement sequence (for example, slip, slip, roll, reset) and the matching stop-short feeds.

Athlete sets stance with the cue "Get set first."

Feeder runs the feeds; the athlete answers with the sequence in order and returns to stance at the end.

The sequence repeats as fatigue builds; the coach compares late repeats with the first ones.

Coach gives one short cue for the first thing that breaks.
what_good_looks_like:
The sequence keeps the same order and size late as early.
Stance holds under the moving head.
The athlete is back in stance at the end of every sequence.
Breathing keeps going.
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: Set position for power transfer with load verification
target_behavior: establishing proper position before initiating offensive actions
purpose: Defense builds protective instincts. Tuesday stabilizes the set-check-punch sequence through repetitive drilling.
standard_setup: Each athlete stands in stance across a taped floor line, with a small pad under the rear foot so loading can be felt. The coach moves along the line and stands side-on to each athlete to see knees, hips and the rear foot.
execution:
Athlete sets stance across the line, rear foot on the pad. Cue: "Get set first."

Coach verifies the load: weight near 50/50, knees soft, rear heel light; the athlete says when the rear foot feels loaded.

On the coach's "go" the athlete transfers weight into one earned straight punch in shadow, the rear foot turning and driving.

Athlete returns to the set stance and the coach re-checks the load before the next rep.
what_good_looks_like:
The load is set and verified before the punch.
Weight transfers onto the lead foot without falling forward.
The punch returns, and the feet recover to the set stance.
The stance after the punch passes the same load check.
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: Defense-set-counter sequences through repeated cycles
target_behavior: establishing proper position before initiating offensive actions
purpose: Head Movement develops evasive capabilities. Tuesday stabilizes the set-check-punch sequence through repetitive drilling.
standard_setup: Pairs facing each other at the range the coach sets; the feeder wears mitts. The coach states the feeder's job before the cycles start and stands to the side of the pairs.
execution:
Feeder throws one attack at the light touch level the coach sets, then waits.

Athlete defends with the slip or the defense the coach names.

Athlete sets: feet, guard, eyes. Cue: "Get set first."

From the set the athlete counters with one earned punch to the feeder's held mitt, or resets.

The pair repeats defense-set-counter cycles for the time the session plan sets; roles swap on the coach's call.
what_good_looks_like:
The system allows offense after defense only when the athlete has recovered enough structure to make a real choice.
Not every defense must produce an immediate counter.
The most important transfer is usable position, not flashy reply.
what_bad_looks_like:
Does the athlete counter because the picture is there or because the athlete expects every defense to become offense.
Can the athlete choose reset or reposition when that is the better answer.
Does the defensive action leave a clear scoring lane or only emotional urgency.
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: Stance width and weight distribution with static holds
target_behavior: maintaining stable positioning throughout all movements
purpose: Footwork establishes positional control. Monday introduces core stance mechanics and static holds.
standard_setup: Open floor, each athlete with room to step in every direction. Tape one straight line on the floor per athlete and a short line at 45 degrees for the rear foot; athletes stand across the line in stance, rear foot on the 45-degree line, facing a mirror or the coach. The coach stands where every athlete's feet and hips can be seen.
execution:
Coach shows the stance once and gives the cue "Get set first."

Athlete steps into stance across the line and holds it still for the time the session plan sets.

During the hold the coach checks width, weight near 50/50, soft knees and a light rear heel, and gives one short cue to fix one thing.

Athlete steps out, shakes off, and sets the stance again from scratch; each new set is one rep.
what_good_looks_like:
Base width roughly shoulder-width plus a half-step, lead foot pointed slightly inward toward the opponent, rear foot at roughly 45°
Weight distribution near 50/50 at rest, shifting to demand — not permanently forward (loses the ability to move back) or permanently back (loses power and forward pressure)
Knees soft and unlocked; hips slightly under, not stuck out behind
Rear heel light, not planted, not up on the toe
what_bad_looks_like: feet too narrow (draw a line on the floor and stand across it); square to the opponent (drill from a taped 45° line); weight on the front foot (drill with the rear foot on a small pad so you can feel loading)
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: Set-breathe-punch under cardio stress with 2-minute continuous flows
target_behavior: establishing proper position before initiating offensive actions
purpose: Punch Integration synthesizes offensive techniques. Thursday maintains set discipline during rapid combination work and fatigue.
standard_setup: Open floor with room to move, a timer, athletes in stance facing the coach. The coach stands where shoulders, chest and feet can be seen.
execution:
Athlete sets and breathes in before the flow starts. Cue: "Get set first."

Athlete runs a 2-minute continuous flow: set, breathe, earned punches in shadow on short exhales, return to stance, breathe in.

The set comes before every punch group, even as breathing gets harder.

Coach gives short breath reminders and watches for breath holding and raised shoulders.

Between flows the athlete restores calm breathing before setting for the next one.
what_good_looks_like:
Breathing should lower unnecessary tension, not create more it.
Action breathing should support movement, timing, and controlled effort during work.
what_bad_looks_like:
Does the athlete hold breath during effort.
Do shoulders rise and stay tight under pressure.
Does breathing become shallow when frustration rises.
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: Weight distribution through punch contact with load checks
target_behavior: maintaining positional integrity during punch execution and impact
purpose: Defense builds protective instincts. Tuesday stabilizes position maintenance through contact drilling.
standard_setup: Each athlete at a heavy bag or a held mitt at punching range, standing across a taped floor line with a small pad under the rear foot so loading can be felt. The coach stands side-on, where knees, hips and the rear foot can be seen.
execution:
Athlete sets stance at the target with weight near 50/50; the coach checks the load. Cue: "Get set first."

Athlete punches the target, the weight moving forward through contact without falling forward.

Athlete returns to stance and the coach checks the load again: back near 50/50, knees soft, rear heel light.

Coach gives one short cue to fix one thing before the next punch.
what_good_looks_like: Weight distribution near 50/50 at rest, shifting to demand — not permanently forward (loses the ability to move back) or permanently back (loses power and forward pressure)
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: Dependable defensive responses with consistent guard positioning
target_behavior: consistent, reliable execution of all learned skills across varying conditions and fatigue levels
purpose: Defense builds protective instincts. Monday introduces consistency standards across all skill domains.
standard_setup: Pairs in stance at a distance where shadowed feeds stop well short; one partner feeds, one defends. The coach stands side-on, where the defender's guard and feet can be seen after every response.
execution:
Coach gives the cue "Get set first."; the defender sets the guard: lead hand at cheek height with the elbow in, rear hand at the jaw.

Feeder shows stop-short shadow feeds at a steady pace; the defender answers each with one defensive response.

After every response the guard returns to the same position by default, without being told.

Coach checks the guard after each response and gives one brief cue when it comes back in a different place.

Partners swap roles at the coach's call, after the time the session plan sets.
what_good_looks_like:
Lead hand at cheek/eyebrow height, elbow in front of the ribs, not flared
Rear hand at the jaw, elbow tight to the ribs
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: Position during extended drill sets with 2-minute rounds
target_behavior: maintaining stable positioning throughout all movements
purpose: Footwork establishes positional control. Thursday tests position maintenance under sustained effort and fatigue.
standard_setup: Open floor with room to move; a timer the whole group can hear. The coach stands where every athlete's feet can be seen.
execution:
Coach gives the cue "Get set first." before each round.

Athletes work 2-minute rounds of the week's stance and stepping work (holds, forward-back steps, called sequences), as the session plan sets.

Coach calls freezes during the round, checks stance at each one, and gives one short cue.

Between rounds athletes recover with a few calm breaths and re-set stance before the next round.

Coach notes what breaks first as the rounds go on.
what_good_looks_like:
Stance width, weight and feet look the same late in the round as early
Athlete arrives in stance at every freeze
Slower is fine; a broken stance is not
Athlete still answers one cue late in the round
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: Action-breath organization with tactical pacing
target_behavior: deliberate action sequencing and tactical organization of offensive and defensive combinations
purpose: Punch Integration synthesizes offensive techniques. Wednesday applies tactical sequencing under coach-called scenarios and decision points.
standard_setup: Open floor with room for each athlete, working in shadow. The coach stands where shoulders and breathing can be seen and calls the scenarios.
execution:
Coach calls tactical scenarios with a pace (for example, slow probing, then a quick exchange, then a reset).

Athlete sets stance with the cue "Get set first."

Athlete breathes out sharply with each action and breathes in during the slower moments.

Athlete matches the breathing to the called pace: steady in slow work, sharp exhales in quick work, a calm breath at each reset.

Coach changes the pace on purpose and checks that the breath follows.
what_good_looks_like:
Breathing should lower unnecessary tension, not create more it.
Action breathing should support movement, timing, and controlled effort during work.
what_bad_looks_like:
Does the athlete hold breath during effort.
Do shoulders rise and stay tight under pressure.
Does breathing become shallow when frustration rises.
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: Stabilize fast transitions with control through repeated rapid sequences
target_behavior: execution tempo while maintaining technical control and positional discipline
purpose: Footwork establishes positional control. Tuesday stabilizes faster tempo execution through repetition at elevated pace.
standard_setup: Open floor with a tape line or cones per athlete marking forward, back and side directions. The coach stands side-on, where feet and hips can be seen through each change of direction.
execution:
Coach gives the cue "Get set first." and sets one short sequence of direction changes.

Athlete repeats the same sequence at an elevated pace, moving in stance without crossing the feet.

At the end of each sequence the athlete stops in stance; the coach checks the finish.

Coach keeps the sequence the same so the transitions settle at the faster pace, and gives one brief cue when a transition breaks.

Athlete works for the time the session plan sets.
what_good_looks_like:
Stance survives every change of direction at the faster pace.
The feet never cross and the athlete does not bounce off both feet at once.
Each sequence ends in stance, ready to move again.
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: Reliable performance under variable conditions including pace changes and partner rotations
target_behavior: consistent, reliable execution of all learned skills across varying conditions and fatigue levels
purpose: Head Movement develops evasive capabilities. Wednesday applies consistent execution under coach-called mixed scenarios and unpredictable patterns.
standard_setup: Pairs in stance at a distance where shadowed feeds stop well short; one partner feeds, one moves the head. The coach stands side-on to the defenders and calls the pace changes and rotations.
execution:
Coach gives the cue "Get set first." and states the feeder's job: shadowed feeds that stop short, at the pace the coach calls.

Defender answers each feed with small head movement and is back in shape before the next.

Coach changes the pace up and down during the round; the head movement stays the same.

At planned points, after a set, the coach calls a partner rotation and the drill restarts with a new feeder.

Athletes work for the time the session plan sets; one brief cue when form changes.
what_good_looks_like:
Head movement stays small and balanced through every pace change.
It looks the same with each new partner.
The defender recovers stance and eyes after each movement.
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: Pivot-guard reset combinations
target_behavior: controlled movement with clean stops, emphasizing deceleration and balance recovery
purpose: Defense builds protective instincts. Monday introduces directional stepping with deliberate stops.
standard_setup: Open floor; a tape cross or a cone per athlete as the pivot spot, with a target line to face. The coach stands where feet and hands can be seen.
execution:
Coach gives the cue "Get set first." and athletes set stance and guard.

Athlete pivots on the lead foot, the rear foot travelling, and stops facing the new line.

Athlete resets guard and stance at the stop: lead hand at cheek/eyebrow height, rear hand at the jaw.

Coach calls short combinations of pivots and steps; the athlete resets after each part.

Coach checks each reset and gives one short cue; continue for the time the session plan sets.
what_good_looks_like:
Lead hand at cheek/eyebrow height, elbow in front of the ribs, not flared
Rear hand at the jaw, elbow tight to the ribs
what_bad_looks_like: Can the athlete pivot or change angle without collapsing posture.
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: Controlled speed during live work with coach-called rapid-fire sequences
target_behavior: execution tempo while maintaining technical control and positional discipline
purpose: Footwork establishes positional control. Wednesday applies speed with control under coach-called rapid sequences.
standard_setup: Pairs facing each other in stance at working distance inside a marked area; partners move as a live picture and may give the light, technical touch the coach sets. The coach stands outside the area, where both partners' feet can be seen, and calls the sequences.
execution:
Coach gives the cue "Get set first." and states each partner's job before the round.

Partners move live; the coach calls short rapid-fire footwork sequences (for example step in, step out, angle) and the athlete answers each call at once.

After each sequence the athlete is in stance, guard up, facing the partner; the partner gives the light, technical touch the coach sets.

Calls get quicker only while the athlete keeps position; when position is given up for speed, the coach gives one brief cue and slows the calls.

Partners swap roles at the coach's call, after the time the session plan sets.
what_good_looks_like:
Every called sequence ends in stance, balanced, facing the partner, guard up.
Speed comes from quicker recognition of the call, not from rushing the feet.
The athlete changes speed on purpose, not emotionally.
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: Planned footwork sequences with defined start-middle-end structure
target_behavior: deliberate action sequencing and tactical organization of offensive and defensive combinations
purpose: Footwork establishes positional control. Monday introduces planned action sequences with clear beginning and end points.
standard_setup: Open floor with a tape mark or cone for a start spot and an end spot per athlete. The coach stands where every athlete's start and end can be seen.
execution:
Coach shows one planned footwork sequence and names its start, middle and end.

Athlete sets stance on the start mark with the cue "Get set first."

Athlete moves through the middle steps in order at a controlled pace, staying in stance.

Athlete arrives on the end mark and freezes in stance to show the sequence is finished.

Athlete walks back to the start; the coach gives one short cue before the next run.
what_good_looks_like:
Every run starts set and ends set, on the marks.
The middle steps come in the planned order with no extra steps.
Stance holds throughout: feet uncrossed, guard and eyes up.
The end is a clear stop, not a drift.
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns

name: Defense-to-offense transitions with clear phase separation
target_behavior: deliberate action sequencing and tactical organization of offensive and defensive combinations
purpose: Head Movement develops evasive capabilities. Monday introduces planned action sequences with clear beginning and end points.
standard_setup: Pairs face each other at a distance where neither athlete's punches reach; the feeder's attacks and the athlete's counters stop short. The coach stands side-on to see each phase.
execution:
Athlete sets stance with the cue "Get set first."

Defense phase: the feeder throws one stop-short punch and the athlete makes one defense with the head.

Recovery phase: the athlete visibly returns to stance, breath and eyes; a short pause marks the line between phases.

Offense phase: the athlete throws a planned counter that stops short, or resets if the picture is closed.

Athlete ends set, and the coach checks that each phase was clear before the next rep.
what_good_looks_like:
The system allows offense after defense only when the athlete has recovered enough structure to make a real choice.
Not every defense must produce an immediate counter.
The most important transfer is usable position, not flashy reply.
what_bad_looks_like:
Does the athlete counter because the picture is there or because the athlete expects every defense to become offense.
Can the athlete choose reset or reposition when that is the better answer.
Does the defensive action leave a clear scoring lane or only emotional urgency.
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: Speed punching with set maintenance through rapid but grounded strikes
target_behavior: execution tempo while maintaining technical control and positional discipline
purpose: Defense builds protective instincts. Monday introduces increased speed within controlled parameters.
standard_setup: Open floor, each athlete in stance with room to punch in the air; no partner or target. The coach stands side-on, where the feet, hips and non-punching hand can be seen.
execution:
Coach gives the cue "Get set first."; the athlete sets stance and guard before any punch.

Athlete throws single fast straight punches in the air, bringing each one straight back to guard with the feet grounded.

Athlete freezes after each punch so the coach can check that the set is still there: base, guard and eyes.

Athlete raises punch speed only while the set holds; when it breaks, the coach gives one brief cue and the athlete slows back down.

Athlete works for the time the session plan sets.
what_good_looks_like:
Punches are fast and come back faster than they go out.
Feet stay grounded; the stance does not lean or fall in.
The other hand stays at guard and the set is visible before the next punch.
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: Organized movement during drill work with coach-called tactical sequences
target_behavior: deliberate action sequencing and tactical organization of offensive and defensive combinations
purpose: Footwork establishes positional control. Wednesday applies tactical sequencing under coach-called scenarios and decision points.
standard_setup: Open floor with cones or tape for reference spots; athletes work in shadow or opposite a partner who moves but never touches. The coach stands where everyone can hear the calls and be seen.
execution:
Coach explains the calls first: each call names a short tactical movement sequence (for example, angle off and reset, or step in and hold).

Athlete sets stance with the cue "Get set first."

On each call, the athlete runs the named sequence and finishes on a clear spot in stance.

Between calls the athlete moves lightly in stance, ready for the next call.

Coach keeps calls short and gives one short cue after a sequence when needed.
what_good_looks_like:
The athlete answers the call straight away, without guessing ahead.
Each called sequence runs in order and ends on a clear spot in stance.
Movement between calls stays organized, not wandering.
Stance holds through every sequence.
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: Step-stop-check in all directions with coach verification
target_behavior: controlled movement with clean stops, emphasizing deceleration and balance recovery
purpose: Footwork establishes positional control. Monday introduces directional stepping with deliberate stops.
standard_setup: Open floor with room to step in all directions; a tape cross on the floor per athlete marks the start spot. The coach stands in front, where every athlete's feet can be seen.
execution:
Coach gives the cue "Get set first." and athletes set stance on the cross.

Athlete takes one step in a direction (forward, back, left, right or a diagonal) and stops dead in stance.

Athlete holds the stop while the coach checks feet, width and balance and either confirms it or gives one short cue.

Athlete steps in the next direction only after the check; work through all directions for the time the session plan sets.
what_good_looks_like:
Forward and backward on a line — lead foot moves first going forward, rear foot first going back, never crossing, never bouncing off both feet at once
Lateral both directions, same logic
Staying in stance while moving in all four directions and all diagonals
what_bad_looks_like:
Does the athlete arrive in stance after moving.
Do feet cross, drift, freeze, or over-step under simple demands.
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: Parry-catch-hold combinations
target_behavior: controlled movement with clean stops, emphasizing deceleration and balance recovery
purpose: Defense builds protective instincts. Tuesday stabilizes multi-directional movement patterns through repetition.
standard_setup: Pairs facing each other at jab range; one feeds slow, light jabs and one defends. The coach stands to the side of the pairs, where both gloves can be seen.
execution:
Coach states the feeder's job (slow, light jabs at the set pace, nothing harder) and gives the cue "Get set first."

Feeder throws a slow, light jab; the athlete catches it in the rear glove or parries it with a small turn of the glove, as the coach calls.

Athlete holds the catch or parry position in stance for a moment, guard intact, then returns the hand to guard.

Coach calls short combinations (for example catch, parry, catch) and gives one short cue; after the time the session plan sets, roles switch.
what_good_looks_like: Catching the jab with the rear glove
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: High guard positioning and elbow placement with partner checks
target_behavior: maintaining stable positioning throughout all movements
purpose: Defense builds protective instincts. Monday introduces core stance mechanics and static holds.
standard_setup: Athletes in pairs, one holding the guard and one checking, standing at arm's length and facing each other. The coach stands to the side of the pairs, where hands and elbows can be seen.
execution:
Coach shows the high guard once, states the checker's job in one line, and gives the cue "Get set first."

Athlete sets stance and guard: lead hand at cheek/eyebrow height, rear hand at the jaw, elbows in front of and tight to the ribs, and holds it still.

Checker gives light glove checks on the guard at the points the coach sets and names one thing that moved.

Athlete fixes it without dropping the hands and holds again for the time the session plan sets.

Roles switch.
what_good_looks_like:
Lead hand at cheek/eyebrow height, elbow in front of the ribs, not flared
Rear hand at the jaw, elbow tight to the ribs
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: Stance through offensive chains with continuous position verification
target_behavior: maintaining positional integrity during punch execution and impact
purpose: Defense builds protective instincts. Wednesday applies positional discipline during combination work with targets.
standard_setup: Each athlete at a heavy bag or held mitts with room to step, a tape line on the floor marking where the feet start. The coach stands side-on, where stance can be seen through the whole chain.
execution:
Athlete sets stance. Cue: "Get set first."

Coach calls an offensive chain; the athlete throws it on the target.

Coach or holder verifies position during the chain and at its end, naming the link where stance broke, if it did.

Athlete finishes each chain in stance before the next call.
what_good_looks_like:
Base width roughly shoulder-width plus a half-step, lead foot pointed slightly inward toward the opponent, rear foot at roughly 45°
Weight distribution near 50/50 at rest, shifting to demand — not permanently forward (loses the ability to move back) or permanently back (loses power and forward pressure)
Knees soft and unlocked; hips slightly under, not stuck out behind
Rear heel light, not planted, not up on the toe
what_bad_looks_like: feet too narrow (draw a line on the floor and stand across it); square to the opponent (drill from a taped 45° line); weight on the front foot (drill with the rear foot on a small pad so you can feel loading)
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: Quick execution under fatigue with sustained speed
target_behavior: execution tempo while maintaining technical control and positional discipline
purpose: Head Movement develops evasive capabilities. Thursday maintains controlled speed during extended high-tempo rounds under fatigue.
standard_setup: Athletes in stance facing the coach or a mirror, each with room for a short step. The coach stands side-on, where head path, feet and guard can be seen through the round.
execution:
Coach gives the cue "Get set first." and starts the round.

Athlete moves the head off the line and back on the coach's calls, keeping each movement quick and small.

Coach keeps the calls coming at a sustained speed through the round; the athlete recovers shape after every movement.

When fatigue makes the movements big or slow to recover, or the guard drops, the coach gives one brief cue.

Athlete works for the time the session plan sets.
what_good_looks_like:
Head movement stays small and quick late in the round.
The guard stays up and stance recovers after each movement.
Speed may drop a little; form does not break.
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: Breathing through incoming volume with controlled inhale-exhale cycles
target_behavior: composure and measured responses during defensive scenarios and incoming pressure
purpose: Defense builds protective instincts. Monday introduces controlled breathing and relaxed defensive postures under simulated pressure.
standard_setup: Pairs face each other at close guard range; the athlete stands in stance with a high guard and the partner gives light, technical touches where the coach sets them. The coach stands where the athlete's shoulders and face can be seen, to watch the breathing.
execution:
Coach gives a short breath reminder and the cue "Get set first." before the set starts.

Partner feeds a steady run of light, technical touches where the coach set them; the athlete keeps stance and guard.

Athlete breathes out as each touch arrives and takes a controlled breath in during the gaps.

Athlete keeps shoulders down and jaw loose while the touches keep coming.

Partner stops on the coach's call; the athlete recovers with a few calm breaths before the next set.
what_good_looks_like:
Breathing should lower unnecessary tension, not create more it.
Action breathing should support movement, timing, and controlled effort during work.
what_bad_looks_like:
Does the athlete hold breath during effort.
Do shoulders rise and stay tight under pressure.
Does breathing become shallow when frustration rises.
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: Quick-breath-reset at higher tempo
target_behavior: execution tempo while maintaining technical control and positional discipline
purpose: Punch Integration synthesizes offensive techniques. Monday introduces increased speed within controlled parameters.
standard_setup: Open floor, each athlete in stance with room to shadow box. The coach stands where shoulders and jaw can be seen and breathing can be heard.
execution:
Coach gives the cue "Get set first."; the athlete sets stance and takes a calm breath.

Athlete throws a short shadow burst at a higher tempo, with a short sharp exhale on each punch.

At the end of the burst the athlete resets: stance, guard and eyes back, and one or two calm breaths with the shoulders down.

Coach starts the next burst only when the reset is visible; tempo rises only while the breath reset still lands.

Athlete repeats burst and reset for the time the session plan sets.

Breathing should lower unnecessary tension, not create more it.
Action breathing should support movement, timing, and controlled effort during work.
what_bad_looks_like:
Does the athlete hold breath during effort.
Do shoulders rise and stay tight under pressure.
Does breathing become shallow when frustration rises.
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

target_behavior: composure and measured responses during defensive scenarios and incoming pressure
purpose: Defense builds protective instincts. Thursday maintains defensive composure during high-volume, extended defensive sequences.
standard_setup: Pairs with room to move; the partner feeds light, technical touches where the coach sets them, in continuous 2-minute cycles on a timer. The coach stands side-on to see shoulders, feet and the clock.
execution:
Athlete sets stance with the cue "Get set first."

Partner feeds continuous light, technical touches for the 2-minute cycle; the athlete defends with small, relaxed movements of feet, head and guard.

Athlete stays loose between actions and breathes out with each defensive action.

Coach compares movement late in the cycle with early in the cycle and gives one short cue.

Athlete recovers between cycles with a few calm breaths and starts the next cycle set.
what_good_looks_like:
Defensive movements stay small and loose through the whole cycle.
Shoulders stay down and breathing keeps going.
Movement late in the cycle matches movement early in the cycle.
Guard and stance are back in place after every action.
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: Breath-punch-return timing with controlled pacing
target_behavior: maintaining positional integrity during punch execution and impact
purpose: Punch Integration synthesizes offensive techniques. Tuesday stabilizes position maintenance through contact drilling.
standard_setup: Open floor or a bag, athletes in stance facing the coach, with room to punch. The coach stands in front and sets the pace by call or clap.
execution:
Athlete sets stance and breathes in. Cue: "Get set first."

Athlete punches on a short exhale and returns to stance.

Athlete breathes in on the return; the next punch waits until the return is complete.

Coach sets a controlled pace by calling or clapping each rep, and slows it when the timing slips.
what_good_looks_like:
Breathing should lower unnecessary tension, not create more it.
Action breathing should support movement, timing, and controlled effort during work.
what_bad_looks_like:
Does the athlete hold breath during effort.
Do shoulders rise and stay tight under pressure.
Does breathing become shallow when frustration rises.
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: Positional discipline during extended rounds with 3-minute continuous mitt work
target_behavior: maintaining positional integrity during punch execution and impact
purpose: Footwork establishes positional control. Thursday maintains stance integrity during extended offensive sequences under fatigue.
standard_setup: The coach or a trained holder in mitts, the athlete in stance with room to move, and a timer. The holder presents clear, still targets and moves only when it serves the lesson.
execution:
Holder and athlete work a 3-minute continuous mitt round.

Holder feeds the day's lesson with short calls and still targets; the athlete punches and moves, finishing each action in stance.

Holder keeps the athlete to the stance standard, with resets and exits, through the whole round, not only to finishing punches.

Late in the round the coach watches for what breaks first and gives one short cue.

Between rounds the athlete restores breathing and stance before the next round.
what_good_looks_like:
Stance and guard still work late in the round, even if speed drops.
Every action finishes in position, not in a flurry.
Feet stay under the body as the athlete moves between targets.
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: Consistent breathing through all actions with regulated rhythm
target_behavior: consistent, reliable execution of all learned skills across varying conditions and fatigue levels
purpose: Punch Integration synthesizes offensive techniques. Monday introduces consistency standards across all skill domains.
standard_setup: Open floor, athletes in stance with room to move and shadow box. The coach stands where shoulders can be seen and breathing heard.
execution:
Coach gives the cue "Get set first."; the athlete sets stance and breathes calmly.

Athlete works through each kind of action in turn (footwork, head movement, defence, punches), exhaling on each action and breathing in the gaps.

Coach checks that the breathing rhythm is the same in every kind of action.

When breathing changes (held, shallow or the shoulders rising), the coach gives one brief breath cue.

Athlete works for the time the session plan sets.
what_good_looks_like:
Breathing should lower unnecessary tension, not create more it.
Action breathing should support movement, timing, and controlled effort during work.
what_bad_looks_like:
Does the athlete hold breath during effort.
Do shoulders rise and stay tight under pressure.
Does breathing become shallow when frustration rises.
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: Slip-counter without position loss using partner verification
target_behavior: maintaining positional integrity during punch execution and impact
purpose: Head Movement develops evasive capabilities. Monday introduces punch delivery while preserving stance structure.
standard_setup: Pairs facing each other at a distance where the feeder's straight stops short of the athlete; the feeder wears mitts. The coach stands to the side of the pairs, where the slip, the counter and the athlete's feet can be seen.
execution:
Feeder throws a single straight that stops short of the athlete.

Athlete slips and counters with one punch to the feeder's held mitt.

Athlete freezes after the counter; the feeder verifies position out loud (feet, guard, chin), saying "good" or the one thing that slipped.

Coach confirms or corrects with one short cue, then the pair repeats; roles swap on the coach's call.
what_good_looks_like:
The system allows offense after defense only when the athlete has recovered enough structure to make a real choice.
Not every defense must produce an immediate counter.
The most important transfer is usable position, not flashy reply.
what_bad_looks_like:
Does the athlete counter because the picture is there or because the athlete expects every defense to become offense.
Can the athlete choose reset or reposition when that is the better answer.
Does the defensive action leave a clear scoring lane or only emotional urgency.
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: Roll-under-return-stop sequences with tempo control
target_behavior: controlled movement with clean stops, emphasizing deceleration and balance recovery
purpose: Head Movement develops evasive capabilities. Tuesday stabilizes multi-directional movement patterns through repetition.
standard_setup: Athletes in stance with room to bend and rise; no equipment and no partner. The coach stands to the side, where knees, hips and head can be seen.
execution:
Coach gives the cue "Get set first." and sets the tempo (slow first, then steady).

Athlete rolls under an imagined hook: bends the knees, shifts weight toward the rear foot and moves the head under and across, eyes up.

Athlete comes back up to stance on the other side and stops still, guard up.

Coach checks the stop and gives one short cue; the next roll starts only on the coach's tempo.

Continue for the time the session plan sets.
what_good_looks_like:
The roll comes from bending the knees, not the waist
Head moves under and across, off the centerline, and the eyes stay up
Athlete comes up in stance and stops still, guard up
Each roll matches the tempo the coach sets
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: Position maintenance during target combos with coach-called 3-5 punch sequences on mitts
target_behavior: maintaining positional integrity during punch execution and impact
purpose: Footwork establishes positional control. Wednesday applies positional discipline during combination work with targets.
standard_setup: The coach or a trained holder wears mitts; the athlete stands in stance at punching range with room to step. The holder presents clear, still targets and stands where the athlete's feet can be seen at each finish.
execution:
Athlete sets stance in front of the holder. Cue: "Get set first."

Holder calls a 3-5 punch sequence and shows the mitts for it.

Athlete throws the sequence on the mitts and finishes back in stance, feet under the body.

Holder waits to call again until the athlete's position is back; if position broke, the holder stops the feed and rebuilds the rep with one cue.
what_good_looks_like:
Feet stay under the body through all 3-5 punches.
Each sequence finishes in stance with the guard back.
No reaching or leaning to the mitts.
The next sequence starts from position, not momentum.
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: Slip-return-freeze mechanic with partner observation
target_behavior: controlled movement with clean stops, emphasizing deceleration and balance recovery
purpose: Head Movement develops evasive capabilities. Monday introduces directional stepping with deliberate stops.
standard_setup: Athletes in pairs: one works and one observes, standing in front at arm's length. The coach stands to the side of the pairs, where heads and feet can be seen.
execution:
Coach states the observer's job in one line (watch head, feet and guard, name one thing) and gives the cue "Get set first."

Athlete slips to one side, returns to centre, and freezes in stance with the guard up.

Observer checks the freeze and names one thing; any touch is a light glove touch at the point the coach sets.

Athlete repeats to the other side; after the time the session plan sets, roles switch.
what_good_looks_like:
Slip is small, from the legs and trunk, and the head comes straight back to centre
Athlete stops dead in stance at the freeze, with no drift or extra step
Guard is up and eyes are on the partner at the freeze
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: Exhale-punch-reset breathing cycle
target_behavior: maintaining positional integrity during punch execution and impact
purpose: Punch Integration synthesizes offensive techniques. Monday introduces punch delivery while preserving stance structure.
standard_setup: Open floor, athletes in stance facing the coach or a mirror, with room to punch in shadow. The coach stands in front, where shoulders, chest and feet can be seen.
execution:
Athlete sets stance and breathes in. Cue: "Get set first."

Athlete throws one punch in shadow on a short sharp exhale.

Athlete resets to stance and breathes in during the reset.

The exhale-punch-reset cycle repeats at a steady rhythm for the time the session plan sets; the coach cues the breath when it drifts.
what_good_looks_like:
Breathing should lower unnecessary tension, not create more it.
Action breathing should support movement, timing, and controlled effort during work.
what_bad_looks_like:
Does the athlete hold breath during effort.
Do shoulders rise and stay tight under pressure.
Does breathing become shallow when frustration rises.
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: Clean stops during flow drills with continuous 3-minute rounds
target_behavior: controlled movement with clean stops, emphasizing deceleration and balance recovery
purpose: Footwork establishes positional control. Thursday maintains movement quality and clean stops during extended sequences.
standard_setup: Open floor with room to move in all directions; a timer the whole group can hear. The coach stands where every athlete's feet can be seen.
execution:
Coach gives the cue "Get set first." before each round.

Athletes flow through continuous movement for 3-minute rounds (steps, pivots, direction changes), as the session plan sets.

Coach calls stops during the round; each stop must be clean, in stance, with no drift.

Coach gives one short cue and notes what breaks first as the rounds go on.

Between rounds athletes recover with a few calm breaths and re-set.
what_good_looks_like:
Athlete stops clean in stance on every call, late in the round as well as early
No drift or extra step after the stop
Movement stays in stance through the continuous work; slower is fine, broken is not
what_bad_looks_like:
Does the athlete arrive in stance after moving.
Do feet cross, drift, freeze, or over-step under simple demands.
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: Calm lateral movement under pressure through side-to-side flow drills
target_behavior: composure and measured responses during defensive scenarios and incoming pressure
purpose: Footwork establishes positional control. Tuesday stabilizes calm defensive responses through progressive intensity drilling.
standard_setup: One floor line per pair running side to side, with room along it; the athlete stands in stance on the line and the partner faces them and moves along it to set the pressure, never touching. The coach stands in front, far enough back to see every pair's feet.
execution:
Athlete sets stance on the line with the cue "Get set first."

Partner moves side to side along the line; the athlete mirrors with lateral steps, the foot nearest the direction of travel moving first, feet never crossing.

Athlete keeps one steady pace and breathes out with the steps.

Coach raises the pressure step by step (partner pace, then direction changes) only while the athlete stays calm and in stance.

On the coach's stop, the athlete holds stance before the next flow.
what_good_looks_like:
Forward and backward on a line — lead foot moves first going forward, rear foot first going back, never crossing, never bouncing off both feet at once
Lateral both directions, same logic
what_bad_looks_like: Do feet cross, drift, freeze, or over-step under simple demands.
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: Composed defense during live drill work with coach-called attack sequences
target_behavior: composure and measured responses during defensive scenarios and incoming pressure
purpose: Footwork establishes positional control. Wednesday applies composed defense under live coach-called attack patterns.
standard_setup: Pairs in an open area big enough to step in every direction; the partner delivers each called attack with light, technical touches where the coach sets them. The coach stands where both athletes' feet can be seen and calls each attack sequence aloud.
execution:
Athlete sets stance with the cue "Get set first."

Coach calls a short attack sequence; the partner delivers it with light, technical touches at the called pace.

Athlete defends with the feet first, stepping off the line or out of range, and keeps the guard up for anything the feet do not solve.

After the sequence the athlete arrives in stance facing the partner, breathes out, and is ready for the next call.

Coach gives one short cue between sequences.
what_good_looks_like:
The feet take the athlete off the line before the hands have to work.
The athlete arrives in stance, facing the partner, after every sequence.
Breathing and face stay calm; no rushing or jumping between calls.
The athlete waits for the attack instead of guessing.
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: Consistent stance recovery in counter work under fatigue
target_behavior: maintaining positional integrity during punch execution and impact
purpose: Head Movement develops evasive capabilities. Thursday maintains stance integrity during extended offensive sequences under fatigue.
standard_setup: Pairs facing each other at a distance where the feeder's attacks stop short of the athlete; the feeder wears mitts, with a timer. The coach stands to the side and runs the fatigue block the session plan sets before the check.
execution:
The pair runs the defense-counter check fresh first; the coach notes the athlete's normal recovery.

After the fatigue block the session plan sets, the feeder throws single attacks that stop short of the athlete.

Athlete defends, counters to the feeder's held mitt, and recovers to stance before the next feed. Cue: "Get set first."

Coach compares recovery with the fresh check and names the first thing that breaks.
what_good_looks_like:
The system allows offense after defense only when the athlete has recovered enough structure to make a real choice.
Not every defense must produce an immediate counter.
The most important transfer is usable position, not flashy reply.
what_bad_looks_like:
Does the athlete counter because the picture is there or because the athlete expects every defense to become offense.
Can the athlete choose reset or reposition when that is the better answer.
Does the defensive action leave a clear scoring lane or only emotional urgency.
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: Guard height through fatigue with extended rounds
target_behavior: maintaining stable positioning throughout all movements
purpose: Defense builds protective instincts. Thursday tests position maintenance under sustained effort and fatigue.
standard_setup: Open floor with room to move; a timer the whole group can hear. The coach stands where hands and elbows can be seen.
execution:
Coach gives the cue "Get set first." and athletes set stance and high guard.

Athletes work extended rounds of movement (steps, slips, pattern work) with the guard held high, as the session plan sets.

Coach calls guard checks during the round; at each one the lead hand is at cheek/eyebrow height and the rear hand at the jaw.

Coach gives one short cue and notes when the guard first starts to drop.

Between rounds athletes recover with a few calm breaths and re-set.
what_good_looks_like:
Lead hand at cheek/eyebrow height, elbow in front of the ribs, not flared
Rear hand at the jaw, elbow tight to the ribs
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: Position verification during combo work with coach-called 2-4 punch sequences
target_behavior: establishing proper position before initiating offensive actions
purpose: Footwork establishes positional control. Wednesday applies setting mechanics under coach-called offensive opportunities.
standard_setup: Open floor, athletes in rows facing the coach with room to step. The coach stands in front, calls each sequence, and can see the start and finish position of every athlete.
execution:
Athlete sets stance and the coach verifies the position before calling. Cue: "Get set first."

Coach calls a 2-4 punch sequence from punches the athlete has earned.

Athlete throws the sequence in shadow and finishes back in stance.

Athlete holds the finish while the coach verifies feet, guard and chin, then the coach calls the next sequence.
what_good_looks_like:
Position is verified before every call.
Each sequence finishes in stance, not leaning or square.
Feet stay under the body through the punches.
The next sequence starts only from a set.
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: Calm counter selection under fatigue with measured offensive responses
target_behavior: composure and measured responses during defensive scenarios and incoming pressure
purpose: Head Movement develops evasive capabilities. Thursday maintains defensive composure during high-volume, extended defensive sequences.
standard_setup: Pairs face each other at a distance where neither athlete's punches reach; the feeder's attacks and the athlete's counters both stop short. Run when the athletes are already tired, at the point the session plan sets. The coach stands side-on.
execution:
Athlete sets stance with the cue "Get set first."

Feeder attacks with stop-short punches; the athlete defends with head movement and recovers shape.

Athlete selects one measured response: a counter the coach has set, stopping short, or a reset or move when no counter is on.

Athlete breathes out with the counter and returns to stance before the next feed.

Coach keeps the choice simple enough to see whether the athlete chose well.
what_good_looks_like:
The system allows offense after defense only when the athlete has recovered enough structure to make a real choice.
Not every defense must produce an immediate counter.
The most important transfer is usable position, not flashy reply.
what_bad_looks_like:
Does the athlete counter because the picture is there or because the athlete expects every defense to become offense.
Can the athlete choose reset or reposition when that is the better answer.
Does the defensive action leave a clear scoring lane or only emotional urgency.
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: Organized execution during complex flow with multi-phase 5-6 action sequences
target_behavior: deliberate action sequencing and tactical organization of offensive and defensive combinations
purpose: Footwork establishes positional control. Thursday maintains organized execution during complex, extended sequences under fatigue.
standard_setup: Open floor with cones or tape for reference spots; athletes work in shadow. Run late in the session, at the point the session plan sets, so the athletes work tired. The coach stands where everyone's feet can be seen.
execution:
Coach shows one 5-6 action sequence in phases (for example, move in, punch, angle off, reset) and names each phase.

Athlete sets stance with the cue "Get set first."

Athlete runs the full sequence in order, keeping stance between every action, and ends set on a clear spot.

Athlete repeats the same sequence as fatigue builds; slower is fine, but the order and the stance stay the same.

Coach watches for the first action to break and gives one short cue for it.
what_good_looks_like:
Every phase of the sequence is still there late in the work, in order.
Stance holds between actions; feet never cross.
The sequence ends set on its spot each time.
Speed may drop; structure does not.
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: Breath-hold at stop points
target_behavior: controlled movement with clean stops, emphasizing deceleration and balance recovery
purpose: Punch Integration synthesizes offensive techniques. Tuesday stabilizes multi-directional movement patterns through repetition.
standard_setup: Athletes in stance with room to step in all directions. The coach stands where shoulders can be seen and breathing can be heard.
execution:
Coach gives the cue "Get set first." and athletes set stance.

Athlete steps in the direction the coach sets and stops in stance.

At the stop point the athlete takes a calm breath in and holds it briefly while checking stance, then breathes out before moving again.

Athlete breathes normally while moving; the hold belongs to the stop only.

Coach watches for the hold spilling into the movement or tight, raised shoulders, and gives one short cue.
what_good_looks_like:
Breathing should lower unnecessary tension, not create more it.
Action breathing should support movement, timing, and controlled effort during work.
what_bad_looks_like:
Does the athlete hold breath during effort.

name: Reliable technical standards with coach verification at each station
target_behavior: consistent, reliable execution of all learned skills across varying conditions and fatigue levels
purpose: Defense builds protective instincts. Tuesday stabilizes reliable performance through repetition under varying conditions.
standard_setup: A small number of defence stations, each with one clear purpose (for example guard recovery, slip and return, exit). A coach or assistant stands at each station to verify the standard.
execution:
Coach gives the cue "Get set first." and names the standard at each station.

Athletes work a station solo or in pairs; at any station with a feeder, feeds are shadowed and stop short.

The station coach verifies each athlete against that station's standard before they move on.

Athletes rotate at the coach's call at the end of a set; one brief cue at a station when the standard is not met.

Athletes work the stations for the time the session plan sets.
what_good_looks_like:
The athlete meets each station's standard, verified by the coach there.
The same defensive quality shows at every station, not only one.
Each defence ends back in shape, guard up.
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: Breath with stop points in 3-4 action flows
target_behavior: controlled movement with clean stops, emphasizing deceleration and balance recovery
purpose: Punch Integration synthesizes offensive techniques. Wednesday applies clean stopping mechanics under coach-called direction changes.
standard_setup: Athletes in stance with room to step, pivot and slip; athletes face the coach. The coach stands where shoulders can be seen and breathing can be heard.
execution:
Coach gives the cue "Get set first." and athletes set stance.

Coach calls a 3-4 action flow of steps, pivots and slips (no punches) with a stop point.

Athlete breathes out short on each action and, at each stop point, breathes in calmly in stance.

Coach watches for held breath or rising shoulders and gives one short cue.

Coach calls the next flow; continue for the time the session plan sets.
what_good_looks_like:
Breathing should lower unnecessary tension, not create more it.
Action breathing should support movement, timing, and controlled effort during work.
what_bad_looks_like:
Does the athlete hold breath during effort.
Do shoulders rise and stay tight under pressure.
Does breathing become shallow when frustration rises.
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: Technical quality at elevated tempo through extended rapid sequences
target_behavior: execution tempo while maintaining technical control and positional discipline
purpose: Defense builds protective instincts. Thursday maintains controlled speed during extended high-tempo rounds under fatigue.
standard_setup: Open floor, athletes in stance with room to shadow box. The coach stands side-on, calls the sequences and watches feet, guard and the finish of each.
execution:
Coach gives the cue "Get set first." and calls a rapid sequence of punches and defensive moves.

Athlete works the sequence in the air at an elevated tempo, each punch back to guard and each defence small.

Coach keeps calling sequences without long breaks, so the tempo stays high through the extended set.

Athlete ends each sequence in stance with the guard up; when quality drops, the coach gives one brief cue and shortens the next sequence.

Athlete works for the time the session plan sets.
what_good_looks_like:
Stance and guard stay working late in the set, even if speed drops.
Every punch returns to guard and every defence stays small.
Each sequence ends in recognisable posture, ready for the next.
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: Composure during extended defense rounds with 3-minute high-volume feeds
target_behavior: composure and measured responses during defensive scenarios and incoming pressure
purpose: Footwork establishes positional control. Thursday maintains defensive composure during high-volume, extended defensive sequences.
standard_setup: Pairs in an open area with room to move; the partner feeds light, technical touches where the coach sets them, in 3-minute rounds on a timer. The coach stands where both athletes' feet and the clock can be seen.
execution:
Athlete sets stance with the cue "Get set first."

Partner feeds a high volume of light, technical touches through the 3-minute round; the athlete defends mainly with the feet, stepping off the line and out of range.

Athlete keeps stance, breath and eyes connected through the whole round and resets after each burst.

Coach watches for the first thing that breaks as the round goes on and gives one short cue for it.

Between rounds the athlete recovers with a few calm breaths.
what_good_looks_like:
Footwork late in the round looks like footwork early in the round: slower is fine, broken is not.
The athlete keeps stepping off the line instead of standing and covering.
Eyes stay on the partner and breathing stays steady.
Each burst ends with a reset in stance.
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: Stop-reset breathing under fatigue with repeated effort cycles
target_behavior: controlled movement with clean stops, emphasizing deceleration and balance recovery
purpose: Punch Integration synthesizes offensive techniques. Thursday maintains movement quality and clean stops during extended sequences.
standard_setup: Open floor with room to move; a timer the group can hear. The coach stands where posture and shoulders can be seen.
execution:
Coach gives the cue "Get set first."

Athletes work repeated effort cycles (a burst of movement, then a called stop), as the session plan sets.

At each stop the athlete resets stance and recovers with a few calm breaths, breathing out first.

Coach coaches the reset as closely as the burst: posture, breath and eyes back before the next cycle.

Coach gives one short cue and notes when the reset first starts to fail.
what_good_looks_like:
Breathing should lower unnecessary tension, not create more it.
Action breathing should support movement, timing, and controlled effort during work.
what_bad_looks_like:
Does the athlete hold breath during effort.
Do shoulders rise and stay tight under pressure.
Does breathing become shallow when frustration rises.
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: Slip left-right from centerline with wall drill
target_behavior: maintaining stable positioning throughout all movements
purpose: Head Movement develops evasive capabilities. Tuesday reinforces positioning through repetition drills.
standard_setup: Each athlete stands in stance facing a wall, a little more than arm's length away, with a vertical tape line on the wall at head height marking the centerline. The coach stands to the side, where head, hips and knees can be seen.
execution:
Coach shows one slip each way and gives the cue "Get set first."

Athlete sets stance with the head lined up on the tape line.

Athlete slips left, moving from the legs and trunk so the head travels a small distance off the line, then returns to the line and stops in stance.

Athlete slips right the same way, returns and stops.

Coach gives one short cue per rep; the athlete repeats left and right for the time the session plan sets.
what_good_looks_like:
Head moves a small distance off the centerline and comes straight back
Movement comes from the legs and trunk, not just the neck
Stance and eyes stay usable through the slip
Athlete stops in stance on the line after each return
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: Guard during multi-step defense patterns
target_behavior: maintaining stable positioning throughout all movements
purpose: Defense builds protective instincts. Wednesday applies positional control under coach-called combinations.
standard_setup: Open floor with room to step and slip in every direction; athletes face the coach. The coach stands in front, where hands and elbows can be seen.
execution:
Coach gives the cue "Get set first." and athletes set stance and high guard.

Coach calls a defense pattern of a few steps (for example step back, slip, step to the side).

Athlete moves through the pattern with the guard held high: lead hand at cheek/eyebrow height, rear hand at the jaw.

Athlete freezes at the end of the pattern; the coach checks the guard and gives one short cue.

Coach calls the next pattern; continue for the time the session plan sets.
what_good_looks_like:
Lead hand at cheek/eyebrow height, elbow in front of the ribs, not flared
Rear hand at the jaw, elbow tight to the ribs
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: Retreat footwork without panic steps using measured backward movement
target_behavior: composure and measured responses during defensive scenarios and incoming pressure
purpose: Footwork establishes positional control. Monday introduces controlled breathing and relaxed defensive postures under simulated pressure.
standard_setup: One straight floor line per pair, with room behind the athlete to step back along it. The athlete stands on the line in stance; the partner faces them at a distance the coach sets and walks forward along the line to give the pressure, never touching. The coach stands side-on to the line to see feet and hips.
execution:
Coach gives the cue "Get set first." and the athlete sets stance on the line.

Partner steps forward slowly; the athlete answers each partner step with one measured step back, rear foot first and lead foot following, feet never crossing.

Athlete breathes out with each step and keeps eyes on the partner, not the floor.

Partner stops; the athlete stops in stance and holds it until the coach sees it set, then the partner walks forward again.

Coach gives one short cue between passes to fix one thing.
what_good_looks_like: Forward and backward on a line — lead foot moves first going forward, rear foot first going back, never crossing, never bouncing off both feet at once
what_bad_looks_like: Do feet cross, drift, freeze, or over-step under simple demands.
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: Load-shift-punch from set stance
target_behavior: establishing proper position before initiating offensive actions
purpose: Defense builds protective instincts. Monday introduces deliberate set position checks before any punch.
standard_setup: Open floor, a straight tape line per athlete; athletes stand across the line in stance, facing the coach or a mirror. The coach stands side-on, where knees, hips and the rear foot can be seen as weight shifts.
execution:
Athlete sets stance across the line and the coach checks it. Cue: "Get set first."

Athlete loads: knees soft, weight near 50/50, guard up.

Athlete shifts weight forward as one earned straight punch goes out in shadow, without falling forward, and the hand returns on the same line.

Athlete freezes in the set stance so the coach can check feet, hips and guard.

Coach gives one short cue and the athlete re-sets for the next rep.
what_good_looks_like:
Stance is set and checked before any load.
Weight moves forward with the punch and the athlete does not fall forward.
On a rear straight the rear foot turns and drives; the hand returns to guard on the same line.
The athlete finishes in the same set stance.
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: Stance check before multi-punch with timed holds
target_behavior: establishing proper position before initiating offensive actions
purpose: Footwork establishes positional control. Tuesday stabilizes the set-check-punch sequence through repetitive drilling.
standard_setup: Open floor, one straight tape line per athlete and a short line at 45 degrees for the rear foot; athletes stand across the line in stance, facing a mirror or the coach. The coach stands where every athlete's feet and hips can be seen.
execution:
Athlete sets stance across the line and holds it still for the time the session plan sets.

During the hold the coach checks width, weight, knees, rear heel and guard, and gives one short cue. Cue: "Get set first."

On the coach's "go" the athlete throws a short multi-punch of earned punches in shadow and returns to the same stance.

Athlete holds again; this hold is the check before the next multi-punch.

Each hold-punch-hold is one rep.
what_good_looks_like:
Base width roughly shoulder-width plus a half-step, lead foot pointed slightly inward toward the opponent, rear foot at roughly 45°
Weight distribution near 50/50 at rest, shifting to demand — not permanently forward (loses the ability to move back) or permanently back (loses power and forward pressure)
Knees soft and unlocked; hips slightly under, not stuck out behind
Rear heel light, not planted, not up on the toe
what_bad_looks_like: feet too narrow (draw a line on the floor and stand across it); square to the opponent (drill from a taped 45° line); weight on the front foot (drill with the rear foot on a small pad so you can feel loading)
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.
