name: Faster footwork with position check using accelerated but verified movements
target_behavior: execution tempo while maintaining technical control and positional discipline
purpose: Footwork establishes positional control. Monday introduces increased speed within controlled parameters.
standard_setup: Open floor with a straight tape line per athlete and room to step forward, back and to both sides. Athletes start in stance on the line; the coach stands side-on to the lines, where feet, hips and guard can all be seen.
execution:
Coach gives the cue "Get set first." and the athlete sets stance on the line.

Athlete steps a short footwork pattern at normal pace and freezes in stance on the coach's call; the coach checks the freeze.

Athlete repeats the same pattern a little faster each time, freezing in stance at the end; speed goes up only while every freeze is clean.

When position is lost for speed, the coach gives one brief cue and the athlete drops back to the last pace that held.

Athlete keeps working for the time the session plan sets.
what_good_looks_like:
Every freeze lands in stance: feet not crossed, base not narrowed, guard up, eyes forward.
Speed rises only as far as the freeze stays clean.
The head stays level while the feet move, with no bouncing off both feet at once.
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: Combination organization under pressure with clear punch groupings
target_behavior: deliberate action sequencing and tactical organization of offensive and defensive combinations
purpose: Defense builds protective instincts. Wednesday applies tactical sequencing under coach-called scenarios and decision points.
standard_setup: Pairs with the partner holding mitts; the partner applies pressure between groupings with light, technical touches where the coach sets them. The coach stands side-on to see each grouping and its finish.
execution:
Coach calls a scenario and a punch grouping (a short combination to the mitts, then a defense or exit).

Athlete sets stance with the cue "Get set first."

Athlete throws the called grouping to the mitts as one clear unit, then finishes with a defensive action or an exit.

Partner presses with light, technical touches between groupings; the athlete answers the pressure, re-sets, and waits for the next call.

Coach checks that each grouping had a clear start and end and gives one short cue.
what_good_looks_like: Every combination ends with either a defensive action or an exit, never with the boxer standing still admiring the work
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: Reliable execution under maximum effort with program-culminating intensity
target_behavior: consistent, reliable execution of all learned skills across varying conditions and fatigue levels
purpose: Head Movement develops evasive capabilities. Thursday maintains performance reliability during extended, demanding final-week testing rounds.
standard_setup: Athletes in stance, each facing the coach or a partner who shadows feeds that stop well short. The coach stands side-on, where head path, feet and guard can be seen through the round.
execution:
Coach gives the cue "Get set first."

Athlete works head movement at maximum effort through the round, answering each call or stop-short feed.

Athlete recovers shape after every movement, however hard the effort.

Coach compares late-round head movement with the fresh version and notes the first thing that fails.

Athlete works for the time the session plan sets; one brief cue when form slips.
what_good_looks_like:
At maximum effort the head movement is still small and recovers to stance.
Each movement ends in a return, exit or reset from a usable position.
Speed may drop; form does not break.
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: Continuous slip-return cycles for endurance
target_behavior: maintaining stable positioning throughout all movements
purpose: Head Movement develops evasive capabilities. Thursday tests position maintenance under sustained effort and fatigue.
standard_setup: Athletes in stance facing the coach or a mirror, with room to slip left and right; a timer the group can hear. The coach stands to the side, where heads and knees can be seen.
execution:
Coach gives the cue "Get set first."

Athlete slips left, returns to centre, slips right, returns, in a steady continuous rhythm for the time the session plan sets.

Each slip stays small and comes from the legs and trunk; each return lands in stance with the guard up.

Coach calls a freeze during the work, checks stance and guard, and gives one short cue.

Between bouts athletes recover with a few calm breaths and re-set.
what_good_looks_like:
Slips stay small and level late in the work, the same as early
Every return lands in stance with the guard up
The rhythm may slow, but the slip does not get bigger or sloppier
Breathing stays steady, not held
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: Rapid defense with technical integrity maintaining defensive form
target_behavior: execution tempo while maintaining technical control and positional discipline
purpose: Head Movement develops evasive capabilities. Tuesday stabilizes faster tempo execution through repetition at elevated pace.
standard_setup: Pairs in stance at a distance where a shadowed straight punch stops well short of the face; one partner feeds, one defends. The coach stands side-on, where the defender's head, feet and guard can be seen.
execution:
Coach gives the cue "Get set first." and states the feeder's job: shadowed straight punches that stop short, at a steady rhythm.

Defender answers each feed with one small defence (a slip or a roll) and is back in shape before the next.

Feeder raises the pace in steps while the defender's form holds; the feed never touches.

When the defence grows, the guard drops or the stance breaks, the coach gives one brief cue and the pace comes back down.

Partners swap roles at the coach's call, at the end of a set, after the time the session plan sets.
what_good_looks_like:
Each defence is small and keeps stance and eyes on the feeder.
The defender is back in shape before the next feed arrives.
Defensive form at the fast pace looks the same as at the slow pace.
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: Breath marking between action phases
target_behavior: deliberate action sequencing and tactical organization of offensive and defensive combinations
purpose: Punch Integration synthesizes offensive techniques. Monday introduces planned action sequences with clear beginning and end points.
standard_setup: Open floor with room for each athlete to move, working in shadow or facing a partner who stands out of reach. The coach stands where athletes' shoulders and breathing can be seen.
execution:
Coach names a planned sequence in phases (for example, a defensive move, then a short combination, then an exit).

Athlete sets stance with the cue "Get set first."

Athlete breathes out sharply with each action inside a phase.

Between phases the athlete marks the change with one controlled breath before starting the next phase.

Athlete ends set, and the coach checks that each phase change had its breath mark.
what_good_looks_like:
Breathing should lower unnecessary tension, not create more it.
Action breathing should support movement, timing, and controlled effort during work.
what_bad_looks_like:
Does the athlete hold breath during effort.
Do shoulders rise and stay tight under pressure.
Does breathing become shallow when frustration rises.
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: Consistent breathing under repeated 4-5 action flows
target_behavior: maintaining stable positioning throughout all movements
purpose: Punch Integration synthesizes offensive techniques. Thursday tests position maintenance under sustained effort and fatigue.
standard_setup: Athletes in stance with room to step and slip; athletes face the coach. The coach stands where shoulders can be seen and breathing can be heard.
execution:
Coach gives the cue "Get set first."

Coach calls a 4-5 action flow of steps, slips and guard shifts (no punches) and the athletes repeat it.

Athlete breathes out short on each action and in calmly between flows, the same pattern every repeat.

Coach watches for held breath, rising shoulders or shallow breathing as the repeats go on, and gives one short cue.

Between bouts athletes recover with a few calm breaths.
what_good_looks_like:
Breathing should lower unnecessary tension, not create more it.
Action breathing should support movement, timing, and controlled effort during work.
what_bad_looks_like:
Does the athlete hold breath during effort.
Do shoulders rise and stay tight under pressure.
Does breathing become shallow when frustration rises.
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: Consistent execution across skill areas with cross-domain quality checks
target_behavior: consistent, reliable execution of all learned skills across varying conditions and fatigue levels
purpose: Head Movement develops evasive capabilities. Tuesday stabilizes reliable performance through repetition under varying conditions.
standard_setup: Athletes in stance with room to step and shadow box. The coach stands side-on, where head, feet and guard can be seen together.
execution:
Coach gives the cue "Get set first."

Athlete links head movement with each other skill area in turn: a step, a guard reset, a punch, and a breath.

After each link the coach runs a quick check across the areas: head back to the middle, feet in stance, guard up, breathing steady.

When one area fails, the coach names it with one brief cue and the athlete repeats that link.

Athlete works for the time the session plan sets.
what_good_looks_like:
Head movement, feet, guard and breath all hold in the same rep.
One area does not fail while another is being worked.
Each link finishes in stance, ready for the next.
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: Structured defense-offense chains under live feed with partner escalation
target_behavior: deliberate action sequencing and tactical organization of offensive and defensive combinations
purpose: Head Movement develops evasive capabilities. Wednesday applies tactical sequencing under coach-called scenarios and decision points.
standard_setup: Pairs face each other at a distance where neither athlete's punches reach; the feeder's live attacks and the athlete's counters stop short. The coach stands side-on and controls the escalation.
execution:
Coach names the chain structure (defend, recover, then counter or exit) and how the partner will escalate.

Athlete sets stance with the cue "Get set first."

Feeder feeds live, stop-short attacks; the athlete defends with head movement, recovers, then counters (stopping short) or exits.

Partner escalates step by step (more attacks, less warning) on the coach's word while the chain keeps its structure.

Each chain ends with the athlete in stance, ready to defend again.
what_good_looks_like:
The system allows offense after defense only when the athlete has recovered enough structure to make a real choice.
Not every defense must produce an immediate counter.
The most important transfer is usable position, not flashy reply.
what_bad_looks_like:
Does the athlete counter because the picture is there or because the athlete expects every defense to become offense.
Can the athlete choose reset or reposition when that is the better answer.
Does the defensive action leave a clear scoring lane or only emotional urgency.
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: Direction change on call with 4-6 step combinations
target_behavior: controlled movement with clean stops, emphasizing deceleration and balance recovery
purpose: Footwork establishes positional control. Wednesday applies clean stopping mechanics under coach-called direction changes.
standard_setup: Open floor with room to step in all directions; athletes face the coach. The coach stands in front, where every athlete's feet can be seen.
execution:
Coach gives the cue "Get set first." and athletes set stance.

Coach calls a 4-6 step combination (for example forward, forward, left, back, L-step).

Athlete steps the combination and changes direction on each call without resetting or crossing the feet.

Athlete stops clean in stance at the end; the coach checks and gives one short cue.

Coach calls the next combination; continue for the time the session plan sets.
what_good_looks_like: L-step, small circle steps, and the ability to change direction without resetting
what_bad_looks_like:
Does the athlete arrive in stance after moving.
Do feet cross, drift, freeze, or over-step under simple demands.
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: See-decide-counter without rushing
target_behavior: composure and measured responses during defensive scenarios and incoming pressure
purpose: Punch Integration synthesizes offensive techniques. Monday introduces controlled breathing and relaxed defensive postures under simulated pressure.
standard_setup: Pairs face each other at a distance where neither athlete's punches reach; the feeder throws slow single straights that stop short, and the athlete's counter also stops short. The coach stands side-on to both.
execution:
Coach gives the cue "Get set first."; the athlete sets stance and breathes out.

Feeder throws one slow straight that stops short; the athlete makes one small defense (head off the line, or a step).

Athlete recovers stance, breath and eyes, sees what is there, then decides.

If the picture is open, the athlete throws one counter that stops short; if not, the athlete resets or steps to a better spot.

Coach praises a calm reset as much as a clean counter.
what_good_looks_like:
The system allows offense after defense only when the athlete has recovered enough structure to make a real choice.
Not every defense must produce an immediate counter.
The most important transfer is usable position, not flashy reply.
what_bad_looks_like:
Does the athlete counter because the picture is there or because the athlete expects every defense to become offense.
Can the athlete choose reset or reposition when that is the better answer.
Does the defensive action leave a clear scoring lane or only emotional urgency.
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: Set-check-punch footwork with coach approval for each punch
target_behavior: establishing proper position before initiating offensive actions
purpose: Footwork establishes positional control. Monday introduces deliberate set position checks before any punch.
standard_setup: Open floor, athletes in rows with room to step in every direction, each facing the coach or a mirror. The coach stands in front, where every athlete's feet, hands and chin can be seen, so the approval for each punch can be given to each athlete.
execution:
Athlete takes a step (forward, back or to the side) and stops in stance.

Athlete sets: feet, weight, guard and chin, then holds still and looks to the coach.

Coach checks the set and approves with a nod or "go"; without approval the athlete re-sets. Cue: "Get set first."

On approval the athlete throws one punch in shadow and returns to the same stance.

Each step-set-approval-punch is one rep.
what_good_looks_like:
The athlete stops in stance before looking for approval.
Feet, guard and chin are set before the hand moves.
The punch comes only after approval and returns to the same stance.
No punch is thrown without a set.
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: Pivot stepping with squared finish through repeated angles
target_behavior: controlled movement with clean stops, emphasizing deceleration and balance recovery
purpose: Footwork establishes positional control. Tuesday stabilizes multi-directional movement patterns through repetition.
standard_setup: Open floor; a cone or tape cross per athlete as the pivot spot, with a target line to finish facing. The coach stands where the feet can be seen.
execution:
Coach gives the cue "Get set first." and athletes set stance facing the target line.

Athlete pivots on the lead foot, turning the rear foot around it, and finishes in stance lined up to face the target again.

Athlete repeats through the next angle, then pivots on the rear foot the same way.

Coach checks each finish and gives one short cue; continue through repeated angles for the time the session plan sets.
what_good_looks_like: Pivots on the lead foot (turning the rear foot around a fixed lead) and on the rear foot
what_bad_looks_like: Can the athlete pivot or change angle without collapsing posture.
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: Relaxed counters from defense under increasing partner pressure
target_behavior: composure and measured responses during defensive scenarios and incoming pressure
purpose: Head Movement develops evasive capabilities. Wednesday applies composed defense under live coach-called attack patterns.
standard_setup: Pairs face each other at a distance where neither athlete's punches reach; the feeder's attacks stop short and the athlete's counters stop short. The coach stands side-on and sets how far the pressure rises.
execution:
Athlete sets stance with the cue "Get set first."

Feeder attacks with stop-short punches at the pressure the coach sets; the athlete defends with head movement.

Athlete recovers shape, then counters relaxed (loose until the punch, breathing out with it) only when the picture is there; otherwise resets or moves.

Coach raises the partner pressure one step at a time (more feeds, less time between them) while the counters stay relaxed.

Feeder pauses after each exchange until the athlete is set again.
what_good_looks_like:
The system allows offense after defense only when the athlete has recovered enough structure to make a real choice.
Not every defense must produce an immediate counter.
The most important transfer is usable position, not flashy reply.
what_bad_looks_like:
Does the athlete counter because the picture is there or because the athlete expects every defense to become offense.
Can the athlete choose reset or reposition when that is the better answer.
Does the defensive action leave a clear scoring lane or only emotional urgency.
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: Combo footwork patterns through repeated 3-4 step sequences
target_behavior: deliberate action sequencing and tactical organization of offensive and defensive combinations
purpose: Footwork establishes positional control. Tuesday stabilizes organized combination patterns through structured repetition.
standard_setup: Open floor with tape lines or cones as reference marks for each athlete. The coach stands where everyone's feet can be seen.
execution:
Coach shows one 3-4 step footwork pattern (for example, step in, step back, pivot, step out) and names it.

Athlete sets stance with the cue "Get set first."

Athlete runs the pattern in order, ends in stance, and repeats it without stopping to re-think.

Athlete keeps the same steps and pace on every repeat; the coach watches for drift between repeats.

Coach gives one short cue, then the athlete continues the same pattern before a new one is named.
what_good_looks_like:
Each repeat matches the last: same steps, same order, same finish.
Stance holds through every step; feet never cross.
Each pattern ends set before the next repeat.
Pace stays controlled; no speeding up to get through it.
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: Deliberate breath before punch initiation
target_behavior: establishing proper position before initiating offensive actions
purpose: Punch Integration synthesizes offensive techniques. Tuesday stabilizes the set-check-punch sequence through repetitive drilling.
standard_setup: Open floor, athletes in stance facing the coach or a mirror, with room to throw. The coach stands in front, where shoulders, chest and hands can be seen.
execution:
Athlete sets stance and checks it. Cue: "Get set first."

Athlete takes one deliberate breath in, shoulders staying down.

Athlete initiates one earned punch in shadow on a short sharp exhale, or a step if punches are not yet earned.

Athlete breathes in on the return to stance.

The set-breath-punch repeats for the time the session plan sets; the coach gives one cue when the breath is skipped.
what_good_looks_like:
Breathing should lower unnecessary tension, not create more it.
Action breathing should support movement, timing, and controlled effort during work.
what_bad_looks_like:
Does the athlete hold breath during effort.
Do shoulders rise and stay tight under pressure.
Does breathing become shallow when frustration rises.
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: Speed-control balance in combinations with quality rapid strikes
target_behavior: execution tempo while maintaining technical control and positional discipline
purpose: Defense builds protective instincts. Wednesday applies speed with control under coach-called rapid sequences.
standard_setup: Open floor, athletes in stance with room to shadow box combinations. The coach stands side-on and calls the combinations, seeing the feet, guard and finish of each one.
execution:
Coach gives the cue "Get set first." and calls a short combination.

Athlete throws the combination fast in the air, each strike on its line and back to guard.

Athlete finishes every combination with a defensive action or an exit and arrives in stance.

Coach calls the next combination quicker only while strike quality and the finish hold; when speed costs quality, one brief cue and the pace comes back down.

Athlete works for the time the session plan sets.
what_good_looks_like: Every combination ends with either a defensive action or an exit, never with the boxer standing still admiring the work
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: Defensive sequence organization with defined entry-exit points
target_behavior: deliberate action sequencing and tactical organization of offensive and defensive combinations
purpose: Defense builds protective instincts. Tuesday stabilizes organized combination patterns through structured repetition.
standard_setup: Pairs with a tape mark or cone for an entry spot and an exit spot; the feeder's attacks stop short. The coach stands side-on to see both marks.
execution:
Coach names the defensive sequence: where it starts (entry), the defensive actions in order, and where it ends (exit).

Athlete sets stance on the entry mark with the cue "Get set first."

Feeder throws the planned stop-short attacks; the athlete answers with the planned defensive actions in order.

Athlete exits to the named spot and freezes in stance, facing the feeder.

The same sequence repeats until it runs the same way each time.
what_good_looks_like:
Each sequence starts set on the entry mark and ends set on the exit spot.
The defensive actions come in the planned order, small and clean.
The exit arrives in stance, facing the feeder, guard up.
Repeats look the same.
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: Guard recovery to high position after movement
target_behavior: maintaining stable positioning throughout all movements
purpose: Defense builds protective instincts. Tuesday reinforces positioning through repetition drills.
standard_setup: Open floor with room to move a few steps in every direction; no equipment. The coach stands where hands and elbows can be seen at each stop.
execution:
Coach gives the cue "Get set first." and athletes set stance and high guard.

Athlete moves as the coach sets (a few steps, a turn, or loose arm swings) and stops.

On the stop, the athlete brings both hands straight back to the high guard, without being told: lead hand at cheek/eyebrow height, rear hand at the jaw, elbows in.

Coach checks the guard at each stop and gives one short cue; repeat for the time the session plan sets.
what_good_looks_like:
Lead hand at cheek/eyebrow height, elbow in front of the ribs, not flared
Rear hand at the jaw, elbow tight to the ribs
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: Exhale timing on defensive shifts
target_behavior: maintaining stable positioning throughout all movements
purpose: Punch Integration synthesizes offensive techniques. Tuesday reinforces positioning through repetition drills.
standard_setup: Athletes in stance with room to shift a step in any direction; no equipment. The coach stands where shoulders can be seen and breathing can be heard.
execution:
Coach gives the cue "Get set first." and athletes set stance.

Coach names one defensive shift (a small slip, a step back, or a guard shift) and the athlete makes it, breathing out short through the shift.

Athlete returns to stance and breathes in calmly before the next shift.

Coach watches for a held breath or rising shoulders and gives one short cue.

Repeat for the time the session plan sets.
what_good_looks_like:
Breathing should lower unnecessary tension, not create more it.
Action breathing should support movement, timing, and controlled effort during work.
what_bad_looks_like:
Does the athlete hold breath during effort.
Do shoulders rise and stay tight under pressure.
Does breathing become shallow when frustration rises.
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: Reliable head movement in all scenarios with predictable technical execution
target_behavior: consistent, reliable execution of all learned skills across varying conditions and fatigue levels
purpose: Head Movement develops evasive capabilities. Monday introduces consistency standards across all skill domains.
standard_setup: Athletes in stance, each facing the coach or a partner who shadows feeds that stop well short, with room for a short step. The coach stands side-on, where head path, feet and guard can be seen.
execution:
Coach gives the cue "Get set first." and names the head-movement standard: small, from the legs and trunk, back to the middle in stance.

Athlete answers a series of scenarios one at a time: solo on the coach's call, against a stop-short shadow feed, and while moving.

Coach checks that the head movement looks the same in every scenario.

When it changes, the coach gives one brief cue and the athlete repeats that scenario.

Athlete works for the time the session plan sets.
what_good_looks_like:
Head movement is small and the same shape in every scenario.
Stance and eyes are kept through each movement.
The athlete is back in shape after each one.
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: Post-punch recovery with immediate position assessment
target_behavior: maintaining positional integrity during punch execution and impact
purpose: Footwork establishes positional control. Tuesday stabilizes position maintenance through contact drilling.
standard_setup: Each athlete at a heavy bag or a held mitt at punching range. The coach stands side-on, close enough to call the assessment straight after each punch.
execution:
Athlete sets stance at range. Cue: "Get set first."

Athlete punches the target once and recovers at once: hand back to guard, feet back under the body.

Straight away the athlete assesses position (feet, guard, eyes) out loud or by the check the coach sets, and the coach confirms.

If the assessment finds a fault, the athlete fixes it before the next punch.
what_good_looks_like:
Hand return and foot recovery happen together, straight after contact.
Guard and base are visible before the next punch.
The athlete can say what was right or wrong with the position.
The athlete does not push the bag or lean on the target.
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: Consistent footwork across all drills with uniform quality standards
target_behavior: consistent, reliable execution of all learned skills across varying conditions and fatigue levels
purpose: Footwork establishes positional control. Monday introduces consistency standards across all skill domains.
standard_setup: Open floor with tape lines or cones laid out for the footwork drills from earlier weeks. The coach stands side-on, where feet and hips can be seen, and uses the same check at every drill.
execution:
Coach states one footwork standard for the day (stance kept, feet never crossing, arriving in stance) and gives the cue "Get set first."

Athlete works through the footwork drills from earlier weeks one after another.

Coach checks every drill against the same standard, whatever the drill.

When a drill falls short, the coach gives one brief cue and the athlete repeats it until it meets the standard twice in a row.

Athlete works for the time the session plan sets.
what_good_looks_like:
The same stance quality shows in every footwork drill, not only the favourite one.
Feet never cross and each movement finishes in stance.
The athlete repeats it without the coach adding extra cues.
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: Relaxed head movement under slow feed with partner progression
target_behavior: composure and measured responses during defensive scenarios and incoming pressure
purpose: Head Movement develops evasive capabilities. Monday introduces controlled breathing and relaxed defensive postures under simulated pressure.
standard_setup: Pairs face each other at a distance where the feeder's straight punch stops short of the athlete's face; feeds are slow and never touch. The coach stands to the side where both heads and both stances can be seen.
execution:
Coach states the feeder's job before the drill: slow, stop-short feeds, one at a time, no trying to win the drill.

Athlete sets stance with the cue "Get set first." and breathes out slowly before the first feed.

Feeder throws one slow straight that stops short; the athlete moves the head just off the line of the punch and returns to centre in stance.

Athlete keeps shoulders and jaw loose and breathes out with each movement; the feeder waits until the athlete is set again before the next feed.

Coach raises the feed (pace, or the side it comes from) only while the athlete stays relaxed; this is the partner progression.
what_good_looks_like:
The head moves only as far as needed to clear the line, then returns to centre.
Shoulders stay down and breathing keeps going through each feed.
Stance and guard are the same after the movement as before it.
The athlete waits for the feed instead of moving early.
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: Breath control during static holds
target_behavior: maintaining stable positioning throughout all movements
purpose: Punch Integration synthesizes offensive techniques. Monday introduces core stance mechanics and static holds.
standard_setup: Athletes in stance with room to stand still; no equipment. The coach stands where shoulders and chests can be seen.
execution:
Coach gives the cue "Get set first." and athletes set stance.

Athlete holds the static stance and breathes slowly and quietly through the hold, for the time the session plan sets.

Coach watches shoulders and chest; if the breath stops or the shoulders climb, one short cue to breathe out and let the shoulders drop.

Athlete steps out of stance, sets again, and repeats the hold with the same calm breathing.
what_good_looks_like:
Breathing should lower unnecessary tension, not create more it.
Action breathing should support movement, timing, and controlled effort during work.
what_bad_looks_like:
Does the athlete hold breath during effort.
Do shoulders rise and stay tight under pressure.
Does breathing become shallow when frustration rises.
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

execution: uppercut mechanics in shadow boxing or light controlled introduction
what_good_looks_like: Lead and rear uppercuts: knees bending to load, rising through the target, elbow travelling under
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns

name: Consistent execution during final rounds with comprehensive 4-minute test rounds
target_behavior: consistent, reliable execution of all learned skills across varying conditions and fatigue levels
purpose: Footwork establishes positional control. Thursday maintains performance reliability during extended, demanding final-week testing rounds.
standard_setup: Open floor with tape lines or cones and a round timer set to 4-minute rounds. The coach stands side-on with the footwork standards the round will test.
execution:
Coach gives the cue "Get set first." and states the footwork standards the round tests.

Athlete works a 4-minute test round covering the footwork from all eight weeks, on the coach's calls.

Coach checks the same standards early and late in the round and notes the first thing that fails.

Between rounds the athlete recovers breath and posture before the next round.

Coach sets the number of rounds from the session plan.
what_good_looks_like:
Footwork late in the round matches footwork early in the round.
Speed may drop, but stance does not break.
Exits and angles end in the named space, in stance, reset.
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: Slip-return-reset under call with partner feed
target_behavior: maintaining stable positioning throughout all movements
purpose: Head Movement develops evasive capabilities. Wednesday applies positional control under coach-called combinations.
standard_setup: Athletes in pairs facing each other, the feeder standing just outside reach so a slow straight feed stops short of the athlete's head. The coach stands to the side of the pairs, where both heads and feet can be seen.
execution:
Coach states the feeder's job: a slow straight feed on the call that stops short and never touches. Coach gives the cue "Get set first."

Coach calls "left" or "right"; the feeder sends a slow straight toward the athlete's head line, stopping short.

Athlete slips to the called side, returns to centre, and resets in stance with the guard up and eyes on the feeder.

Coach gives one short cue; after the time the session plan sets, roles switch.
what_good_looks_like:
Slip is small and comes from the legs and trunk; the head comes back to centre
Athlete resets in stance with the guard up before the next call
Eyes stay on the feeder through the slip and the reset
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: Linked head movement-counter chains with smooth transitions
target_behavior: deliberate action sequencing and tactical organization of offensive and defensive combinations
purpose: Head Movement develops evasive capabilities. Tuesday stabilizes organized combination patterns through structured repetition.
standard_setup: Pairs face each other at a distance where neither athlete's punches reach; the feeder's attacks and the athlete's counters stop short. The coach stands side-on.
execution:
Coach names the chain (for example, slip, counter, slip, counter) and the feeder's matching stop-short feeds.

Athlete sets stance with the cue "Get set first."

Feeder throws the planned feeds; the athlete moves the head, then counters from where the head movement left them, each counter stopping short.

Athlete flows from each link to the next without stopping, but is back in stance shape before each new link.

The same chain repeats until the transitions are smooth, then the coach names the next chain.
what_good_looks_like:
The system allows offense after defense only when the athlete has recovered enough structure to make a real choice.
Not every defense must produce an immediate counter.
The most important transfer is usable position, not flashy reply.
what_bad_looks_like:
Does the athlete counter because the picture is there or because the athlete expects every defense to become offense.
Can the athlete choose reset or reposition when that is the better answer.
Does the defensive action leave a clear scoring lane or only emotional urgency.
common_errors: Sacrifice position for speed; Skip the set-check sequence; Demonstrate inconsistent breathing patterns
corrections: Coaches should intervene before poor patterns become habitual, using brief verbal cues rather than extended explanations during active drilling.

name: Body shots score 3, head shots 1
target_behavior: Body punching, level changes, entries
purpose: Teaches body punching inside a live round: because a body shot is worth three times a head shot, the boxer is pushed to change levels and find safe entries to the body. Live pressure, one constraint.
standard_setup: Body shots score 3, head shots score 1
execution:
Coach states the rule and the roles before the bell: body shots score 3, head shots score 1, and the coach keeps the score; both boxers work at the pace and contact the coach sets for controlled sparring.

Boxer changes level from the legs, not the waist, to reach the body, entering inside safely with the head off centre.

Boxer exits after the body shot instead of staying low or reaching for more.

Coach stays silent during the round and gives one note in the interval; the round runs for the time the session plan sets.
what_good_looks_like:
Body shots come from a knee bend, with the head off centre.
The boxer enters to the body behind the feet and leaves after scoring.
The guard still protects the head while the boxer works low.

name: Single-shot rounds
target_behavior: Maximum intent per punch, full recovery
purpose: Builds the habit of putting full intent into one punch and recovering completely before the next, so maximal effort never turns into a flurry.
standard_setup: Bag; one maximal punch every 10 s
execution:
Coach sets one bag per athlete and keeps the time; the athlete starts in stance at punching range.

Athlete throws one maximal punch every 10 s, then returns to guard and stance and waits for the next window.

Coach watches that only one punch goes per window; a second punch or a flurry is the drill's failure mode and the coach calls it.

Run 3 × 2 min (the Long Road's prescription).
what_good_looks_like:
Every punch is a full-intent shot, not a push.
Guard and base are back before the next window.
One punch per window, every window.
common_errors: Throwing more than prescribed

name: Rope drill
target_behavior: Lateral rather than backward movement
purpose: Takes away the straight-back retreat in live work: the boxer must stay within reach of a horizontal rope, so pressure has to be solved by moving laterally.
standard_setup: Horizontal rope at shoulder height; must stay within reach
execution:
Coach sets a horizontal rope at shoulder height and the rule: the boxer must stay within reach of it.

Partner pressures at the pace and contact the coach sets for controlled sparring.

Boxer solves pressure by moving laterally along the rope, pivoting and angling off, not by backing away from it.

Coach calls any time the boxer leaves reach of the rope.

Run 4 × 2 min (the Long Road's prescription).
what_good_looks_like:
The boxer stays within reach of the rope for the whole round.
Pressure is met with lateral steps, pivots and angles, finishing in stance facing the partner.
No straight-line backward steps.

name: Isometric holds — flexion, extension, both lateral flexions
target_behavior: Holds the head still against steady pressure in each direction, chin level, without shrugging or leaning the trunk into the push.
purpose: Builds static neck strength in all four directions (forward, back and to each side) as a short block inside the warm-up. Boxing keeps accelerating the head, so the neck is trained on purpose.
standard_setup: Done inside the warm-up. Athlete stands or sits tall, chin level, and presses against their own hand (forehead, back of the head, each side) or a folded pad against a wall. Coach stands side-on to see head and shoulder position.
execution:
Athlete sets posture: tall, chin level, shoulders down.

Athlete presses the head forward into the hand or pad (flexion) and holds without letting the head move.

Athlete repeats the hold backward (extension), then to the left and to the right (both lateral flexions).

Run 3 × 10–15 s each direction, building to 3 × 30 s (the Long Road's prescription).

Athlete then runs one boxing check (stance reset or jab recovery); coach logs the exposure and the first technical degradation.
what_good_looks_like:
The head does not move during the hold.
Chin stays level; shoulders stay down and the trunk does not lean into the push.
The boxing check right after shows no posture collapse, guard loss or stiffness.

name: Diaphragmatic breathing
target_behavior: Breathes from the belly with an exhale longer than the inhale, and uses that breath to settle between rounds without being told.
purpose: Trains slow belly breathing with a long exhale so the athlete can lower tension on purpose, then carries that breath into the rest between rounds until it happens without thinking.
standard_setup: A quiet spot on a mat or bench, away from bag noise. The athlete takes the sitting or lying position the record's first step gives; the coach stands where both hands (belly and chest) can be seen.
execution: Sit or lie with one hand on the belly, one on the chest. The belly hand moves; the chest hand does not - Progress to a 4-2-6 pattern: inhale 4 s, hold 2 s, exhale 6 s. The extended exhale is the parasympathetic driver - Then practise it in the 60-second interval between rounds, on the bag and in sparring, until it is automatic. This is the transfer step everyone omits - Morning and pre-sleep
what_good_looks_like:
The belly hand rises and falls; the chest hand stays still.
The exhale is longer than the inhale and unforced.
Shoulders stay down.
Between rounds the athlete settles in a few calm breaths.

name: Reach-only
target_behavior: Range discipline; exposes over-reaching
purpose: Range discipline with the jab: both boxers may only jab, from jab range, so any over-reaching shows at once.
standard_setup: Both may only jab, from jab range
execution:
Coach sets the rule: both boxers jab only, from jab range, at the pace and contact the coach sets for controlled sparring.

Each jab starts from stance at the boxer's own jab range; the feet adjust the distance, not the arm.

The rear hand stays home on defense.

Coach calls any jab thrown from out of range (reaching, leaning, falling in).

Run 4 × 2 min (the Long Road's prescription).
what_good_looks_like:
Jabs land at full extension from the boxer's own range, without leaning.
The boxer steps to find range instead of reaching for it.
After each jab the hand returns and stance is ready.

name: Combination 1 – 1 – 2
target_behavior: From long range the second jab lands on a different beat from the first, the cross goes in straight behind it, and the athlete leaves by stepping back or pivoting.
purpose: Second jab arrives off-beat; cross behind it
execution:
Coach names the sequence and its exit before the rep: 1 – 1 – 2, then step back or pivot.

Athlete starts in stance at long range (shadow, bag or pads) and throws the first jab.

Athlete lands the second jab off the beat of the first, not as an identical double, and drives the cross straight in behind it.

Athlete leaves the moment the cross lands, stepping back or pivoting, and resets stance and eyes before the next rep.

Coach moves the sequence up the coupling ladder only when it holds at the current rung.
what_good_looks_like:
The two jabs land on different beats, never as one identical double.
The cross goes straight in behind the second jab, without a reach.
The exit starts as the cross lands and ends in stance.

purpose: Target: previously learned material, now with unpredictability.

Every lead-hand shot finds the pad and comes straight back to the guard.
The feet get to the pad's new spot before the hand goes.
Under pressure from the partner the boxer still lands from stance, not by reaching.
The rear hand stays home all round.

name: Guard-height rounds
target_behavior: Keeps the guard at its set height through every round when tired: zero drops.
purpose: Builds guard integrity under fatigue: bag rounds after conditioning, filmed, with guard drops counted, so late-round guard height is trained and measured.
standard_setup: Bag work after conditioning; film it
execution:
Run in the last 15–20 minutes of a session, after conditioning, once the main behavior of the day is already stable.

Athlete works the bag for 3 × 3 min with the guard as the scored constraint: hands back to guard after every punch.

Coach films each round.

Coach (or the athlete) counts guard drops per round from the film; the target is zero.
what_good_looks_like:
Hands come back to guard after every punch, in the last round as in the first.
The count of guard drops per round is zero or falling.
Punches may slow, but the guard does not break.

name: Set-It-Then-Send-It
target_behavior: Every rear hand is set up first and finishes with recovery; no naked rear hand.
purpose: eliminate naked rear hand.
standard_setup: mitt or bag; coach only allows rear hand after setup.
execution: rear hand only after jab, feint, level change, angle, or defensive read.
what_good_looks_like:
Each rear hand comes after a visible setup.
The cross lands with the stance still usable and the head not past the front knee.
The lead hand returns or guards during the punch, and the rear hand recovers to guard, pivot or step-out.
No naked rear hands in the final round.
common_errors: emotional power punch.
corrections: remove rear hand for one minute; rebuild jab/feint.
transfer: counter-entry touch spar.
exit_condition: rear hand has setup and recovery.

name: Combination Feint 1 – 2 – 3
target_behavior: A small, believable feint draws a reaction, the 1 – 2 – 3 goes where that reaction opened space, moving from long to mid range, and the athlete pivots out.
purpose: The feint gathers information and creates space
standard_setup: Feint 1 – 2 – 3
execution:
Coach names the sequence and its exit before the rep: feint, 1 – 2 – 3, then pivot.

Athlete starts in stance at long range (shadow, bag or pads) and shows a small feint (shoulder, hand or foot) without committing weight.

Athlete reads the answer to the feint (on pads, the holder shows one), then throws 1 – 2 – 3 into the space it opened, closing from long to mid range.

Athlete pivots out the moment the hook lands and resets stance and eyes before the next rep.

Coach moves the sequence up the coupling ladder only when it holds at the current rung.
what_good_looks_like:
The feint is visible but the weight never commits.
The 1 – 2 – 3 goes where the reaction opened space, not on a fixed count.
The athlete stays balanced after the feint and pivots out in stance.

name: Thoracic spine mobility
target_behavior: Moves the upper back through extension and rotation with the hips and lower back quiet, then boxes the check afterwards with posture, guard and feet intact and no extra stiffness.
purpose: Keeps the upper back moving in extension and rotation so the shoulder does not have to make up for a stiff thorax when the athlete punches.
standard_setup: Mobility space on the gym floor near a wall, with a mat, and a notebook for the log. The coach stands side-on to see the upper back and the hips.
execution:
Athlete works rotation first, for example thoracic open-books lying on the side with knees stacked, the top arm opening while the eyes follow the hand.

Athlete adds thread the needle on hands and knees, then upper-back extension the coach chooses, keeping the lower back still.

Coach sets and records the amount for the day (exercise, range, time, how hard it felt); there is no fixed dose.

Athlete then runs a short stance-and-jab recovery check and the coach looks for posture, guard and footwork.

Coach logs the result and the next step up or down.
what_good_looks_like:
Rotation comes from the upper back; the hips and lower back stay quiet.
The athlete breathes through each rep instead of forcing range.
On the boxing check afterwards, stance, guard and feet are the same or freer, not stiffer.

name: Muscle buffering / lactate tolerance
target_behavior: Holds output across every hard interval: the last effort stays close to the first, with the last 30 seconds of each genuinely hard.
purpose: stoppages and knockouts are typically preceded by sequences of high-force actions. The boxer who can produce such a sequence, recover, and produce another has a weapon. The boxer who produces one and then needs ninety seconds does not.
standard_setup: Curved treadmill or bike (or another mode where output can be measured), a clock, and a sheet to record each interval's distance, power or speed. Placed at least 24 hours from hard sparring in either direction.
execution:
Athlete runs a fresh check of one assigned boxing task before the set.

Coach sets the target intensity: an effort the athlete can just complete for 2 minutes, with the last 30 seconds genuinely difficult.

Athlete works 2 minutes at that intensity, then recovers actively for 3 minutes; 6–8 repetitions (the Long Road's prescription).

Coach records every interval's output and compares it with the first.

After the set, athlete repeats the same boxing check; coach logs the first breakdown.
what_good_looks_like:
Every interval is completed.
Output in the last intervals stays close to the first.
The last 30 seconds of each effort are genuinely hard, and the boxing check after the set is still trainable.

name: Reverse shot clock
target_behavior: Reading and patience
purpose: Forces reading and patience: for the first 15 s of each round the boxer may not throw, so the round opens with reading the partner, not with punches.
standard_setup: May not throw for the first 15 s of each round
execution:
Coach sets the rule: the boxer may not throw for the first 15 s of each round; the partner works at the pace and contact the coach sets for controlled sparring.

In the first 15 s the boxer moves, defends and reads the partner (range, lead, reactions) while staying loaded.

After the window the boxer may throw, using what was read.

Coach calls the end of the window and any punch thrown inside it.

Run 4 × 2 min (the Long Road's prescription).
what_good_looks_like:
In the no-punch window the boxer stays loaded and organised: stance, guard and feet ready.
The first punches after the window answer something the boxer saw.
No freezing in the window and no rush at its end.

name: Distance denial drill
target_behavior: Denies the partner's preferred range with feet, angle and position while staying in stance, ready to score, reset or deny from where they stand.
purpose: Trains micro-distance from the denying side: the boxer works to stop the partner ever settling at the range the partner wants, using feet and position rather than punch volume.
standard_setup: Ring or open floor, both boxers in sparring kit. The coach tells the partner which range to work for (long, middle or inside) and how fast to work; the coach stands side-on to see the gap between the front feet.
execution: Denial drills: the boxer’s only job is to prevent the partner establishing their preferred distance
what_good_looks_like:
The partner rarely gets set at the range they want.
The boxer solves distance with the feet first and the hands second.
The boxer stays in stance and can score or reset from the spot they take.
No chasing and no straight-line retreat.

name: Shadow with direction calls
target_behavior: Immediate direction change while continuing to punch
purpose: Trains the boxer to change direction the instant the coach calls it without the hands stopping, so moving and punching stay one skill.
standard_setup: Coach calls a direction
execution:
Athlete shadowboxes in open space in stance, punching continuously.

Coach calls a direction (forward, back, left, right); the athlete changes direction at once and keeps punching through the change.

Coach watches the hands at each call; a pause in punching to change direction is the failure mode and gets one short cue.

Run 4 × 2 min (the Long Road's prescription).
what_good_looks_like:
The first step in the new direction comes right on the call.
The hands keep working through every change.
The stance holds in every direction.
common_errors: Stopping punching to change direction

name: 1–2–3 combination progression
target_behavior: Throws 1-2-3 as one connected chain from stance: the straights close the distance, the hook lands from the closed distance, the guard comes back after every punch, and the chain ends in defense or an exit.
purpose: Primary Focus: Slip-counter integration, combination layering, ring control
standard_setup: Open floor with room for each athlete to step and turn, athletes in lines facing the coach. Shadow only: no partner and no contact. The coach stands in front, then walks the lines, where guards and lead feet can be seen.
execution:
Coach demonstrates 1-2-3 slowly and names each punch's job: the straights close the distance, the hook uses the closed distance.

Athlete throws the 1-2-3 in shadow at slow speed and freezes in stance after the hook; coach checks that the guard came back after every punch.

Athlete finishes each 1-2-3 with a defensive move or an exit step instead of standing still.

Coach lets speed rise only while the shape holds, for the time the session plan sets.
what_good_looks_like:
Straight → bent (1-2-3): the straights close distance, the hook exploits the closed distance
Every combination ends with either a defensive action or an exit, never with the boxer standing still admiring the work

name: Switch on the bell
target_behavior: Switches to the mode the coach names at each bell and keeps that mode, with stance and structure, for the whole round.
purpose: Builds working access to a second and third mode: the boxer changes style every round against the same partner, so switching becomes a trained skill and not a last resort.
standard_setup: Ring and timer, the same partner for every round. Before each bell the coach names the mode for the round, for example going forward, going backwards, close range or long range.
execution: “Switch on the bell”: change mode every round against the same partner
what_good_looks_like:
From the first exchange of each round the boxer is plainly in the new mode.
The mode holds for the whole round.
Stance and exits stay clean in the less-preferred mode.
The round stays on its declared purpose; the boxer does not start a different fight.

name: Defense Gives the Punch
target_behavior: Every defensive action leads to a useful next action: a counter, an angle or a reset.
purpose: remove dead defense.
standard_setup: coach feeds one attack cue.
execution: correct defense -> counter -> exit/reset.
what_good_looks_like: defense finishes in position for return

common_errors: slip/roll with no decision.
corrections: repeat same cue until counter/exit is linked.
transfer: constraint spar where scoring begins only after defense.
exit_condition: defense leads to counter, angle, or reset.

name: Grip, forearm and wrist strengthening
target_behavior: Holds a straight wrist and a firm grip in the carries and grip holds, moves the wrist through full, controlled range in the rollers and band work, and boxes the check afterwards with no loss of guard or hand position.
purpose: Builds grip, forearm and wrist strength so the hands and wrists hold their position through training, in the area the Long Road names as boxing's most common injury site.
standard_setup: Strength or mobility area with the kit for the row: carry weights, a wrist roller, a bucket of rice, a band, and a notebook for the log. The coach stands side-on to see the wrists.
execution: Heavy carries, wrist rollers, rice-bucket work, isometric grip holds, wrist extension band work
what_good_looks_like:
Wrists stay straight under load in the carries and grip holds, and the grip does not open early.
Wrist rollers and band work move through full, controlled range, with no jerking.
Posture holds through the carries; shoulders do not hike.
On the boxing check afterwards, guard and fist position are unchanged.

name: Mid-round switch
target_behavior: Live re-planning
purpose: Trains live re-planning: the coach changes the round's constraint at a random point, and the boxer must change approach on the spot.
standard_setup: Coach changes the constraint at a random point mid-round
execution:
Coach starts the round with one constraint the boxer has already trained (for example no jab, no rear hand, or no forward movement).

Boxer and partner spar at the pace and contact the coach sets for controlled sparring.

At a random point the coach calls a new constraint; the boxer switches at once.

Coach watches how fast the boxer changes and whether the new constraint is kept.

Run 5 × 3 min (the Long Road's prescription).
what_good_looks_like:
The boxer changes approach within moments of the call.
The new constraint is kept for the rest of the round.
The boxer stays organised through the switch, without stalling or scrambling.

name: Trap-bar deadlift
target_behavior: Drives the load up with the legs through the floor while the back stays neutral and the hips and shoulders rise together.
purpose: high load tolerance, short learning curve, more upright torso than a straight-bar deadlift so less lumbar shear, and it loads the hip and knee extensors that drive the punch
standard_setup: mid-foot under the handles, shins near the bar, hips higher than a squat but lower than a stiff-leg, chest up, lats engaged, neutral spine
execution: push the floor away rather than pulling the bar up; hips and shoulders rise together; finish tall without hyperextending
what_good_looks_like:
Hips and shoulders rise together from the first pull.
The back stays neutral from start to lockout, with the weight in the mid-foot.
The lift finishes tall without leaning back, and the boxing check after it stays clean.
common_errors: hips shooting up first (load too heavy or hamstring stiffness), rounding at the start (set the lats before pulling), bar drifting forward (weight in the mid-foot, not the toes)
transfer: trains the triple-extension pattern underlying leg drive

name: Guard Recovery Reps
target_behavior: After a light shoulder tap, the athlete returns to a full guard and a balanced stance at once, without flinching and without answering emotionally.
purpose: Build automatic recovery
standard_setup: Partners face each other in stance, guard up, close enough for one to reach the other's shoulder; a partner or the coach gives the tap. The coach stands to the side where the athlete's guard and feet can be seen.
execution: Light shoulder tap → immediate guard reset
what_good_looks_like:
The guard comes back up fast and visibly after every tap.
No flinch and no tapping back.
Stance and balance hold; the eyes stay on the partner.
The athlete is back in shape before the next tap.

name: Circuit work with boxing movements
target_behavior: Every station serves one named purpose, and the assigned boxing technique stays recognisable to the last station.
purpose: Generally low value
standard_setup: Stations of boxing movements (for example shadow, bag, footwork) laid out with a clock and a notebook. The coach names the circuit's one purpose and its conditioning category before it starts, and stands where every station can be seen.
execution:
Coach names the purpose and the one technical target the circuit must keep.

Athlete moves through the stations for the work and rest the session plan sets; the Long Road gives no fixed dose ("Various").

Coach scores the technical target at each station, not the volume.

After the circuit, athlete repeats the same technical check; coach logs clean reps, failed reps and the first failure.
what_good_looks_like:
The athlete can say what the circuit is for.
The assigned technique looks the same at the last station as at the first.
Resets between stations are organised, not wandering.

name: Jab + Slip
target_behavior: Every jab is followed by a small knee-bend slip and a full return to stance before the next rep.
purpose: Links offense to defense: the athlete throws a jab, slips the head to the side by bending the knees, and resets stance, so the switch from punching to defending becomes quick and controlled.
standard_setup: Open floor, athletes spread out in stance with room to move; no partner. The coach stands in front where every athlete's knees, head and guard can be seen.
execution: Jab → Slip → Reset stance.
what_good_looks_like:
The jab extends straight and comes back to the guard.
The slip is small and comes from bending the knees, not leaning.
The guard stays up through the slip.
The athlete is back in stance before the next jab.

name: Hanging leg raise / ab wheel
target_behavior: Builds front-of-trunk strength with controlled reps: the trunk stays braced and the movement comes from control, not swinging.
purpose: Anterior chain strength
standard_setup: A pull-up bar for the hanging leg raise, or an ab wheel on a mat. Coach stands side-on to see the hips and lower back.
execution:
Athlete uses the variant the coach sets: hanging leg raise or ab wheel.

Hanging leg raise: athlete hangs still, braces, raises the legs under control without swinging, then lowers slowly.

Ab wheel: athlete kneels, braces, rolls out only as far as the lower back stays neutral, then pulls back with the trunk.

Run 3 × 8–12 (the Long Road's prescription).

Athlete then runs one boxing check (stance reset or jab recovery); coach logs the first degradation.
what_good_looks_like:
No swinging or momentum; each rep is controlled up and down.
The lower back stays neutral at the far point of the rollout.
The boxing check after the set stays clean.

name: Punching mechanics review
target_behavior: Lands every punch with a straight wrist and aligned fist, and can name the one fault on their own slow-motion clip.
purpose: Uses slow-motion video of the athlete's own bag work to find hand faults at impact (wrong knuckles, bent wrist, poor alignment) so they can be coached out.
standard_setup: Heavy bag and a phone or camera on a stand, side-on to the bag at hand height, recording in slow motion; a notebook. Coach and athlete review the clip on the screen after the round.
execution: Most hand injuries have a technique component — landing on the wrong knuckles, wrist extension at impact, poor alignment. Slow-motion video of bag work reveals this immediately and almost nobody does it
what_good_looks_like:
On the clip the wrist stays straight at impact.
The fist lands square on the knuckles the coach teaches, in line with the forearm.
Each review ends with one named fault and one fix, not a list.

name: Full competition simulation with all of the above
target_behavior: Boxes their own plan and system under full competition conditions, keeping structure, decisions and composure when the result counts.
purpose: The last step of pressure inoculation: rounds run like a bout, with an audience, a visible scoreboard and clock, judges, an announced result and an agreed consequence, so the boxer has already performed under competition pressure before competing.
standard_setup: Ring and timer, a scoreboard and clock the boxers can see, judges, and a small audience. Boxers in competition kit; the coach in the corner.
execution:
Coach agrees the consequence with the boxers before the bout (meaningful, not punitive) and states each boxer's round purpose.

Boxers are called out and box the agreed rounds at open-sparring level, with the score and clock visible.

Between rounds the coach restores breathing and gives one correction and one success condition.

Judges score, the result is announced and the agreed consequence is applied.

Coach reviews one lesson that held and one that broke.
what_good_looks_like:
The boxer keeps the plan and structure when the score or the crowd turns against them.
Between rounds the boxer settles their breathing and takes in one correction.
The rounds look like applied learning, not emotional brawling.
Win or lose, the boxer can say what held and what broke.

name: Slip line progression (slip only → slip + jab → slip + cross)
target_behavior: Slips the head off the line with small, balanced movements from the knees (not the waist) and returns a straight punch off the slip, guard back after every punch.
purpose: Primary Focus: Slip-counter integration, combination layering, ring control
standard_setup:
Side View Diagram:
  Rope Line -----------
  Athlete moves head under rope without bending at waist excessively.
  Emphasis: small slips, balanced feet.
execution:
Athlete stands in stance under the rope line and slips only: the head moves off the line with a small bend of the knees, not the waist.

Athlete moves along the rope, stepping and slipping, keeping the feet balanced.

Athlete adds a jab after each slip (slip + jab), guard back after the punch.

Athlete then slips outside and returns the rear straight (slip + cross), guard back after the punch.

Coach moves the group to the next stage when the slips stay small and balanced.
what_good_looks_like: Slip outside → rear straight

name: Metronome rhythm change
target_behavior: Holds one steady tempo, then changes rhythm the moment the signal comes, keeping stance, balance and eyes.
purpose: Trains deliberate rhythm control: the boxer locks onto a set tempo, then breaks it at once when the beat stops, so tempo changes are chosen and not accidental.
standard_setup: A metronome or metronome app on a speaker loud enough to hear over the gym; shadowboxing space or a bag. The coach holds the device so the beat can be cut without warning, and stands where the boxer's feet and guard can be seen.
execution: Drill: metronome work — box to a metronome for 2 minutes, then have a coach randomly kill the metronome and require immediate rhythm change
what_good_looks_like:
On the beat, punches and steps land with the metronome.
When the beat stops the rhythm changes at once (a break, a pause, a half-beat shot) instead of carrying on in the old tempo.
Balance holds through the change.
The change is chosen, not frantic.

name: Ballistic bench press throw
target_behavior: Moves a light load as fast as possible on every rep, so speed, not grinding, is the training effect.
purpose: Builds upper-body explosive strength, the Long Road's priority quality for the upper body, by pressing a light bar at maximum speed.
standard_setup: A rack with safety pins, a Smith machine, or a landmine setup, so the bar can be released at the top where the equipment allows. Coach stands where the bar path and the athlete's shoulders can be seen.
execution:
Athlete sets up on the bench under the chosen equipment, shoulder blades set.

Athlete lowers the bar under control, then presses it up at maximum velocity, releasing it at the top where the equipment allows.

Athlete resets fully before the next rep.

Run 4 × 3 @ 30–45% 1RM (the Long Road's prescription).

After the set, athlete runs an immediate reset or skill check; coach logs clean explosive reps and the first failure.
what_good_looks_like:
Every rep is pressed at full speed; the bar does not slow near the top.
The athlete resets between reps instead of bouncing.
The reset or skill check right after shows no stance collapse, guard abandonment or delayed reset.

name: Lead-hand-only sparring
target_behavior: Making the lead hand a scoring weapon
purpose: Makes the lead hand a scoring weapon: live rounds where only the lead hand attacks and the rear hand defends, so the boxer learns to score and control range with the jab under real pressure. Live pressure, one constraint.
standard_setup: Constrained live; rear hand defensive only
execution:
Coach sets both boxers' roles before the bell: the boxer may attack only with the lead hand; the rear hand defends only; pace and contact are what the coach sets for controlled sparring.

Partner works to the role the coach assigns, at the same controlled contact.

Boxer steps in to jab, steps out after jabbing and keeps the rear hand home to catch, parry and protect the chin.

Coach calls any rear-hand punch at once; sneaking the rear hand in is the drill's failure mode.

Run 5 × 2 min (the Long Road's prescription, rung 6).
what_good_looks_like:
The lead hand lands clean scoring shots, not pawing touches.
The boxer steps to jab and moves after jabbing instead of standing in front.
The rear hand stays at the chin and only defends.
common_errors: Sneaking the rear hand in

name: Measure both ranges
target_behavior: Knows, against each partner, the distance where their own rear hand lands and where the partner's lands, and can stop on the edge of their own range by eye.
purpose: Finds and marks the two ranges that matter against each partner, where the boxer's rear hand lands and where the partner's does, so the boxer can see the gap between them and learn to live in it.
standard_setup: Open floor with tape and a marker; boxer and partner in stance facing each other, measuring by reaching out slowly, no punches at speed. The coach stands side-on to see the front feet and writes each partner's marks down.
execution: Measure both ranges precisely with each sparring partner and mark them
what_good_looks_like:
Each partner has two marks on the floor: the boxer's rear-hand range and the partner's.
Each range is measured from stance, not by leaning.
The boxer can step to the edge of their own range and stop there without looking down.

name: Round-end sprints
target_behavior: Holds output to the bell: the last 20 s of each bag round at maximal output, with form kept.
purpose: Trains the ability to take the end of a round: the final 20 s of every bag round goes at maximal output.
standard_setup: Final 20 s of every bag round at maximal output
execution:
Applies to every bag round, always (the Long Road's prescription).

Coach calls the final 20 s of each bag round.

Athlete goes to maximal output for the final 20 s: fast, clean punches with guard and stance kept.

Coach watches that output holds through to the bell.
what_good_looks_like:
Output rises or holds in the last 20 s instead of fading.
Punches stay clean: guard returns and stance holds.
The athlete is still organised at the bell.

name: Wall drill
target_behavior: Rotation rather than reaching
purpose: Teaches the punch to get its power from rotation, not from reaching: standing close to a wall takes away over-extension, so the hips and trunk have to do the work.
standard_setup: Standing close to a wall, unable to over-extend
execution:
Athlete stands in stance close enough to a wall that a reaching punch is not possible; the coach checks the distance.

Athlete throws the rear straight by turning the rear foot and hip and letting the shoulder and arm follow, finishing without leaning toward or touching the wall.

Athlete returns to guard on the same line after every punch.

Run 3 × 20 (the Long Road's prescription).
what_good_looks_like:
The punch comes from the rear foot and hip turning, not the arm reaching.
The athlete never pushes off or leans into the wall.
The hand returns through the guard and the stance stays usable.
common_errors: Pushing off the wall

name: Five jabs circuit
target_behavior: Range-finder / power / up-jab / body / blinding, in rotation
purpose: Builds five distinct jabs on the bag (range-finder, power, up-jab, body, blinding), one per round, so each jab has its own purpose and mechanics instead of being the same punch at different speeds.
standard_setup: Bag
execution:
Coach names the jab type for the round before the bell: range-finder, power, up-jab, body or blinding.

Athlete throws only that jab on the bag for the round, with the mechanics that jab needs, and recovers to stance after each one.

Coach checks that the jab looks and works differently from the last round's, not the same punch faster or slower.

Run 5 × 2 min, one jab type per round (the Long Road's prescription).
what_good_looks_like:
Range-finder light and fast; power jab stepping in with weight behind it.
Up-jab rising from low; body jab with a knee bend and the head off the centre line.
Blinding jab loose, from a lower guard, low power.
Every jab comes back to guard with the stance intact.
common_errors: Making all five the same punch at different speeds

name: HRV biofeedback
target_behavior: Breathes at the slow rate the app paces, with a long, smooth exhale, and does it consistently through the week.
purpose: Trains slow paced breathing with live heart-rate feedback from an app and chest strap, so the athlete learns what a calm, regulated breath feels like and can repeat it.
standard_setup: A quiet seat; the chest strap on and paired to the validated app. The coach checks the strap is reading before the set starts. Used only if the device is available.
execution: Resonance-frequency breathing training with a validated app and a chest strap - The evidence is moderate and the practice is harmless; worth doing if you will do it consistently
what_good_looks_like:
Breathing follows the app's pacer smoothly.
The exhale is long and unforced; shoulders stay down.
The athlete keeps the routine across the week.
